items.title: China Publicly Discloses Plan For a Lunar Landing Within Three Years
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, Chinese space officials publicly outlined the most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon "before 2030." Ars Technica reports: China's lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon. According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
 
- An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027
- An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon's surface. Target: 2028
- A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. Target: 2029
- Dual launch of Long March 10 rockets, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to crewed landing mission. Target: "Before 2030" 

The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China's technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface. Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China's space station in low-Earth orbit.

Snap was the last social media company named in the lawsuit to settle the case, which was set for opening arguments this week. Meta resolved claims last week, while Alphabet and TikTok, the other defendants, each also resolved the allegations. Terms of the Snap settlement were undisclosed [...]. 
Earlier this year, a jury found Meta and Google-owned YouTube liable in a landmark social media addiction lawsuit, awarding $6 million in damages to a young woman who alleged the platforms' addictive features harmed her mental health. items.title: Study Claims Vizio Simply Ignores 'Smart' TV Spying Opt Out Requests
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Techdirt: Recently, reports emerged that LG TVs are sniffing around your local network, and even listening to your local environment, even when the TV is purportedly "off." Some of those voice commands were then stored in plain text and uploaded to the internet. LG's response? To deny everything. [...] That latter point is central to a new study out of Northeastern that conducted 5,943 experiments across twelve commercial "smart" TV devices. The researchers found that most smart TVs utilize automatic content recognition (ACR), a technology that captures audio or video snapshots of viewed content and then monetizes that data to help build personalized profiles of viewers.
 
TV makers insist that users are supposed to be able to opt out, but the choice simply doesn't work across a large segment of TVs. Companies like Vizio simply ignored the consumer requests entirely more often than not: "We find that the advertised ACR opt-out fully suppresses ACR-attributable traffic on only four operating systems; on Samsung Tizen traffic consistent with ACR activity persists in more
than 60% of evaluated scenarios, and on Vizio SmartCast a content correlated endpoint hosted on Amazon Kinesis continues to receive traffic in 100% of opted-out scenarios."
 
[...] The researchers say since they can't see the precise scope of what's being collected due to encryption, they're unsure whether Vizio is technically violating its FTC agreement (not that we have a current FTC that would care if they were): "The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint; however, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement." Results of whether opting out of ACR tracking actually stopped ACR tracking were all over the map. Roku, for example, ignores opt-out requests when users are watching Roku's own channels. None of the smart TV vendors track Netflix viewing for fear of violating agreements with the streaming giant. Samsung's opt out function was more likely to actually work when a user was watching antenna broadcasts.
 
On two Smart TV platforms, personal viewing data collected by ACR remains unencrypted, despite years of bad press and scandal on the subject. Many appear to be violating the law, but because U.S. regulatory oversight has been gutted, they see no meaningful accountability. That includes smart TV OS' like VIDAA, which is most prominently found on Hisense and Toshiba smart TVs: "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it. Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can't be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint."

items.title: Music Through Your Cheekbones: How Bone-Conduction Headphones Work and Why They Sound Different
items.author: Reetain Raina
items.content:
Most headphones function in a very simple manner: sound waves created by the headphones propagate through the air into the ear canal and into the inner ear. However, there are some headphones that have a non-traditional approach to producing sound for listening to music. These headphones can deliver sounds through vibrations to the head bones and tissues, thus enabling users to listen to music without inserting earbuds into the ear canals or using bulky headphones that cover them completely.

Such headphones are called bone-conduction headphones, as they produce vibrations in addition to the conventional sounds created by speakers.

It may appear strange, but the science behind this process is fairly simple. In fact, there is always some kind of bone conduction when a person speaks and hears his own voice. Vibrations generated by the act of speaking pass not only through the air but through the body, which explains why the voice that is recorded differs from the voice we hear when speaking.

In addition, transmission of sounds via the head affects how music is being played. In order to explain why this happens, it is necessary to learn more about how these headphones function and how sound vibration turns into music.

First, Understand How Traditional Headphones Deliver Sound

Before diving into the mechanics of bone conduction, it helps to establish exactly how normal headphones work. Understanding this baseline makes the technical jump to bone conduction much easier to follow.

The Journey of Sound Through Your Ears

Headphones are designed based on the principle of air conduction and transmit sound into the inner ear in the following way. First, sound waves are produced from the headphones as a result of a diaphragm's rapid vibration. These waves move through the air inside the ear canal and eventually encounter the eardrum that starts vibrating.

Then, three small bones in the middle ear, called malleus, incus and stapes, amplify the vibrations and pass them on to the cochlea. It is an incredibly small organ located in the inner ear, which has the shape of a snail and contains fluid. Moreover, it consists of a basilar membrane, which separates the liquid inside the cochlea. As the waves move through the liquid, the sensory hair cells convert mechanical energy to the electrical one. Finally, the signals reach the brain through the auditory nerve, which interprets them as sound. However, the eardrum is not the only place for vibrations to get to the cochlea.

How Bone-Conduction Headphones Actually Work

Whereas miniature speakers have been traditionally used, modern consumer bone-conduction headphones make use of transducers that are electromechanical. This is because the main function of these transducers is to convert electrical audio signals to mechanical vibration. This is different from normal headphones since the transducer does not go inside or on the ears. They usually come into contact with the skin around the ear region.

From Electrical Signals to Mechanical Vibrations

Hearing using a bone conduction device is quite distinct from the one used by earbuds. Once the audio signal sent from the computer to the headphones has been received, it gets converted into mechanical waves through the transducer inside. The transducer moves in sync with the skin of your face and the body tissues beneath it.

This vibration travels through the biological parts of your head, without interacting with the outer and middle ear at all. Mechanical energy turns into motion in the cochlear region. From here, the entire process becomes just like any other form of hearing process, where the sensory hair cells detect the motion in the fluid and send signals to the brain through the auditory nerve.

Does Sound Really Travel Through the Skull Bones?

It is easy to picture bone conduction as one simple process involving the skull, but the reality of it is actually quite complicated. The process of transmission of sounds through the head includes more than one pathway operating at once.

As described in the basic research on bone-conducted sounds and their physiology, there are a number of different ways that this is accomplished. Vibrations lead to movement of the fluid within the cochlea, called cochlear fluid inertia, which is one of the main factors that allow us to hear bone-conducted sounds. Also, the small bones of the middle ear react to the vibration of the skull (ossicle inertia). Moreover, the vibrations cause micro-movement of the walls of the cochlea. Surprisingly, vibrations of the skull also produce secondary sound pressure within the ear canal.

Why Bone-Conduction Headphones Sound Different From Regular Headphones

If you have ever tried a pair of bone-conduction headphones, you immediately notice that they do not reproduce sound in exactly the same way as conventional earbuds. The audio often feels different in texture and weight. This variance comes down to the transducers, the physical vibration pathways and how human tissue filters different frequencies.

Bass Doesn't Feel the Same

Bass sounds that have lower frequencies are critical in the listening experience of music in modern times. In the case of regular earphones, changes in air pressure are used effectively in stimulating the eardrum. In the case of bone conduction headphones that people can buy, the sound waves have to fight their way to the cochlea through a combination of skin, cartilage and bone tissues.

Human tissue has a natural tendency to dampen certain mechanical frequencies, thus, the production of bass tones is noticeably less intense. The transducers have to vibrate more in order for bass tones to be produced, thus, there will be a noticeable buzzing and tickling effect on the cheekbones of the listener.

Sound Leakage and Environmental Noise

Since the transducers are placed totally outside of the ear canal and operate by making vibrations outside of the head, part of the acoustic energy is bound to leak out into the air. As a result, there will be sound leakage, which means that people who happen to be sitting close to you can overhear the low-quality music leaking from the earphones. Additionally, the open-ear technology allows all kinds of background noises to get into your ears automatically.

The Engineering Behind Bone-Conduction Headphones

Designing consumer bone-conduction wearables requires engineers to navigate a highly specific set of physical limitations. Building a traditional speaker is mostly about moving ai, building a bone-conduction transducer is about effectively transferring mechanical energy into the human body.

Why Transducer Placement Matters

The issue of positioning the transducer is significantly more complicated than just finding a place where it will be able to vibrate. The exact position of the transducer, the force of its pressure on the skin and the coupling with the underlying tissue will determine the efficiency of vibrations reaching the inner ear.

One particularly intriguing experiment conducted in 2023 on bone conduction hearing via bone conduction headsets revealed precisely this connection. It was found out that vibrating the area near the opening of the ear canal greatly increased bone conduction sensitivity by about 20 dB compared to the classical position of the transducer behind the ear (mastoid bone) with the highest sensitivity increase of up to 40 dB on certain frequencies.

Engineers always find themselves in the midst of a tug-of-war when it comes to trade-offs. The vibration can be enhanced in the transducer, which may result in improved bass and volume, however, very soon, it will result in skin fatigue for the user. A more tight headband provides better mechanical coupling and sound transmission, but it results in a headache due to the pressure exerted on the head.

Why Do Bone-Conduction Headphones Leave Your Ears Open?

The most defining visual characteristic of these headphones is that they leave the ear entirely unobstructed. By resting on the temporal bone or cheekbone, they do not physically block the ear canal in any way.

Understanding the Open-Ear Design

The open ear technology allows normal transfer of environmental sound through the air to your eardrum despite you listening to a podcast or music. It addresses the issue of situational awareness that is faced by a particular user segment. Bicyclists would be able to hear any coming traffic, office workers can listen to music and still be aware of their colleagues and even runners can have spatial awareness around them.

But most importantly, it needs to be realized that having an open ear feature does not mean that it automatically provides you with safety. Listening to loud playback using bone conduction technology may mentally distract the listeners and loud environmental sound would also be enough to mask the audio you are listening to. What's more, no consumer bone conduction headsets provide any kind of passive noise cancellation.

Are Bone-Conduction Headphones Better for Everyone?

It is a mistake to view consumer bone-conduction technology as a direct upgrade or replacement for conventional headphones. Instead, both technologies solve fundamentally different listening problems.

Where Bone Conduction Makes Sense

They are perfect for those people who have trouble wearing regular ear buds because of discomfort or the tendency for them to fall out. They are great options for outdoor sportsmen, urban travelers and anyone else who wants to have their own music soundtrack while staying engaged with reality.

Where Traditional Headphones Still Have an Advantage

If you’re someone who requires high-fidelity sound quality, then the concept of bone conduction won’t work for you. Over-the-ear or in-the-ear headphones have a far more superior performance when it comes to deep bass, wide soundstage and an immersive experience. The one purpose for which bone conduction headphones can’t fulfill their purpose is to cancel the noise of an airplane or noisy café.

The Bigger Picture: Bone Conduction Is More Than Just Another Headphone Technology

In addition to traditional methods of listening to music, the technology of bone conduction is opening new classes of wearable devices for consumers. This is because the bone-conduction system does not occlude the ear canal and it is increasingly becoming an integral part of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses and spatial computing visors.

While using AR glasses, you need your digital data to be laid over the real one. Bone conduction transducers integrated into the arm of smart glasses can provide you with directions, responses of your virtual assistant and even chime notifications without isolating you from your environment. In tactical, outdoors and sports communications, it allows team members to coordinate themselves through voice communication while remaining fully acoustically aware of their environment.

Ultimately, the emergence of bone conduction technology demonstrates an interesting biological phenomenon - the fact that sound doesn’t always have to pass through the ear canal to be audible. This kind of headphones shows how versatile the human auditory system can be in its ability to convert mechanical vibrations via different physical paths into our beloved music.

Although their distinctive transfer method restricts the capabilities of the headphones in terms of bass reproduction and noise isolation, it provides a truly unique combination of digital sound and physical perception. In case our brain can easily process the sound via vibrations transmitted through the skull, what other physical paths could be used by future wearables to change our digital experiences?

items.title: Your AI Agent's Memory Needs Two Clocks
items.author: Rudraj Mehta
items.content:
Consumer agents run for years with the same user. A companion, a coach, or a journaling app collects thousands of small facts, most of which are only true for a while or evolve over time. Things like a race next Sunday, a trial ending in January, a trip last week, etc. With time, the memories stay in the pool even after the event time has passed.

Most setups store what the user said and when the system stored it, and nothing about when it actually happened. And the agent has no way to tell what is still true at retrieval time. For continuity, we will use one running example in this article - a fitness coach app called Stride, with a user named Sam.

Every memory has two clocks.

Event time is when the thing happened: Sam ran the race on Sunday. Write time is when your app got to know about it: during a user’s chat session or during a later data import. Tracking these two independent timelines, when the event happened and when the system learned about it, is , and relational databases have done it for decades. Most memory setups keep only write time, and that holds until the two timelines disagree. They disagree often, and we’ll discuss the list of possible cases here.

Stride has run for two years and wants to import old chats. Sam wrote "I ran my first 10K last weekend" in June 2025. Store it today, and the system reads "last weekend" against today, so the memory becomes "Sam ran a 10K this week," wrong by a year and stuck that way since the import loses the original date. Pass the original conversation time on every write and resolve the phrase against it.

memory.add(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "I ran my first 10K last weekend, finished in 58 minutes."}],
    user_id="sam",
    event_time=1750075200,   # 2025-06-16, the day Sam said it
)

The stored memory now reads "User ran a 10K on the weekend of 2025-06-14 to 2025-06-15," its created date reads June 2025, and a date filter for June 2025 finds it.

2. Time-relevant terms in chats

Sam says "I started the new knee meds yesterday." Resolve the phrase at write time, because only then do you know the actual conversation date, and store the date instead of the word. You also need a precision scale: "yesterday" is a day, "last month" is a month, and you should not invent an exact day from a vague phrase. Pass the exact instant the message was sent so time zones work out. "This morning" sent at 5 AM in Singapore is still the previous day in UTC.

Sam is vegetarian, then starts eating fish. Sam lives in Lisbon, then moves to Berlin. Both were true at different times, and a coach app that mixes them suggests tofu for lunch recommendations in a city Sam doesn’t live in anymore. Do not delete the old fact. It needs to be retained and linked to the new fact to create a chain of events. A user may ask need the current value or the history depending on different cases:

memory.search("Where do I go for dinner this weekend?", user_id="sam")
memory.search("Where did I use to go for my weekend runs last year?", user_id="sam")

4. Facts with an end date

"Training for the Berlin half on Nov 15" should stop affecting responses after Nov 15. "Dry January" ends Jan 31. Certain memories need an expiration setting at the time of writing, and the expiration should hide a memory rather than delete it, because the record still matters for history. The memory needs to stay visible through the date and drop out of search results the day after, with a way to show expired ones on request.

Before each reply, the coach app asks "what did Sam struggle with last week?" or "my knee injury’s progress from July to September." Two tools do different jobs:

  • Filters on actual event times give you hard windows for deterministic questions; that is how a filter on June 2025 would find the memory you created recently in a bulk import.
  • Temporal reranking reorders memories by how well each memory's date fits a natural-language question when an explicit date range is not mentioned. One caution: some queries like "suggest a workout for next week" use a time word as part of the request itself - don’t turn it into a filter.

Pass "now" into each read instead of letting the system decide the time autonomously. A nightly job at 02:00 UTC is morning in Singapore and the previous evening in San Francisco. An eval asking "what would the app have known on 2026-03-21?" should stay fixed as the day changes. A reference date fixes this.

memory.search("What did I eat last night?", user_id="sam", as_of="2025-08-10T12:00:00Z")

7. Old facts crowding out new ones

After 18 months, 2025 knee injury memories continue to match for the keyword "knee." Memory age alone is not a strong enough signal; how often a memory still gets retrieved is a stronger one. Memories need to be retrieved based on usage-based reranking and not directly filtered, so a two-year-old allergy stays reachable while a healed injury drifts down, and comes back up only if Sam specifically mentions the knee again.

Sam says "I told you about my injury and you still pushed me to run hills." You need a way to reliably investigate what the app knew on a given day. Pull every memory written up to that date without any filters, and check whether the injury's creation date precedes the hill session.

For a single memory, its change history should return each write and update with the old text, the new text, and when it changed.

The capabilities to look for

If you build or buy a memory layer for long-running consumer agents, these are the knobs it needs:

Old data with original dates

event-time, duration, and precision parameters on write

linking chain of events, with a current-only filter

an expiry field, plus a way to show expired

created-at filters with required logic operations

reference-date override on search

Stale memories rank lower

usage-based decay on ranking

a created-at filter with per-memory history

The idea is simple: track both event time and write time for every memory with the above parameters and filters, and your app’s memory setup should be able to take care of almost all time-related scenarios.

items.title: Your AI Assistant Is Waiting Around - An AI Agent Goes to Work
items.author: Elnaz Sarraf
items.content:
Something clicked for me the day I stopped treating AI like a really smart search box.

I have been in AI long enough to have built a company in it and exited it. My old company made ROYBI Robot, an AI robot that taught young children language and STEM, the kind of work that drew real press and put me in rooms I never expected to be in. I say that plainly because it explains my impatience: I have watched AI go through its hype cycles from the inside, and most of my relationship with it still looked like this: I ask, it answers, I move on. A vending machine for words. Useful, sure, but I was still doing all the actual work myself. The chasing down, the compiling, the following up. The AI talked. I acted.

Then I learned the difference between an assistant and an agent, and it rearranged how I think about getting things done.

An assistant waits for your instructions and executes them. You hand it step-by-step directions. An agent takes a goal and figures out the steps on its own. You give it an objective and some guardrails, and it goes to work while you do something else entirely.

The textbook definition says an agent is an AI system that perceives its environment, makes decisions, takes actions, and pursues goals with some degree of autonomy. The practical definition is shorter: an agent is an AI that acts instead of just talking.

Here is the analogy that made it click for me. Asking an AI for restaurant recommendations is a chatbot. Hiring someone to research the options, check availability, read the reviews, compare prices, book the table, and put it on your calendar is an agent. Same conversational surface. Completely different animal underneath.

The five things that make an agent an agent.

Not everything wearing the “agent” label earns it. The word gets slapped on anything with a chat box these days. Here is the checklist I actually use:

  1. Perception. It can gather information from its environment: read documents, query a database, watch a feed.
  2. Reasoning. It can work through multi-step problems and decide what to do next.
  3. Action. It can do things, not just suggest them: call APIs, write files, send messages.
  4. Persistence. It keeps context across steps and sessions instead of starting from zero every time.
  5. Goal orientation. It is aimed at an outcome, not just answering prompts.

Run a few familiar tools through that filter, and the picture sharpens fast.

A customer service chatbot that answers questions from a knowledge base? Not really an agent. Give that same bot the ability to check your order in the database, process the refund, update the CRM ticket, and email you a follow-up tomorrow. Now you are talking.

And I am not describing this from the sidelines. This is how I run my work today, with my agents working end to end while I direct them and make the calls that actually need a human.

Same with coding tools. GitHub Copilot finishing your lines as you type is handy, but it is not agentic. A tool like Cursor, which reads your whole codebase, reasons about the architecture, makes changes across multiple files, runs the tests, and iterates on the failures, is acting, remembering, and pursuing a goal. That is much closer to agency.

You do not need all five traits maxed out, by the way. An agent that is strong on three or four of them will still run circles around a plain chatbot. The trick is matching the level of agency to the actual job instead of chasing maximum autonomy for its own sake.

The mindset shift nobody warns you about.

The hard part of agents is not technical. It is mental.

You are used to asking questions and getting answers. With agents, you define goals and turn the AI loose to pursue them. You are used to doing tasks yourself. Now you describe what “done” looks like and let the agent handle the execution.

That transition from doing to directing is subtle, and honestly a little uncomfortable at first. You have to learn to specify outcomes instead of procedures, constraints instead of steps. But once it clicks, you start seeing agent-shaped problems everywhere: the report you compile from six sources every Monday, the competitor blog you check by hand, the inbox triage you do over coffee.

Build your first one today: 20 minutes, no code

The best way to learn agents is to build one. Here is a genuinely useful starter: a research agent that watches a topic for you and emails you a daily digest. Twenty minutes of setup, and it keeps paying you back every morning.

You will need a free Make.com account. Their visual builder shows the agent’s logic as a flowchart, which makes the concepts concrete instead of abstract.

  1. Create a new scenario and add a Schedule module set to run once a day at whatever time you like. This is your agent’s sense of time passing, the thing that kicks off its work cycle.
  2. Put a Filter between the parser and the next step, and configure it to pass through only items published in the last 24 hours. That is your agent deciding what is relevant and ignoring the rest.
  3. Add an AI module (OpenAI or Claude API) that takes each article’s title and description and writes a tight two-ence summary. Raw feed data becomes something you can actually skim.
  4. Add an email module that sends you the compiled digest: title, summary, and link for each item.

Save it, enable it, done. Every day that agent wakes up, scans your topic, filters the noise, summarizes what is new, and lands it in your inbox. Scheduled perception, relevance reasoning, AI as a tool, action to deliver value. Every core agent concept, in one small package you can deploy before lunch.

Two beginner mistakes to dodge. First, do not filter so aggressively that nothing passes through; check the execution history to see what got dropped and loosen up. Second, resist the urge to over-engineer. You do not need complex planning algorithms or production-grade error handling on day one. Build five simple agents before you build one complicated one. Each small build teaches you a pattern, and the patterns compound.

Once you start thinking in agents, the ceiling moves.

Customer service teams run agents that resolve the routine inquiries and escalate only the genuinely hard cases to humans. Development teams have coding agents that implement features from specifications, write the tests, and open pull requests. Marketing teams test dozens of message variants while everyone sleeps.

The interesting part is not even the labor savings. It is the work that becomes possible at all: watching thousands of sources at once, personalizing content for every single user, testing a hundred variations simultaneously. Nobody could do that by hand at any price. Agents do not just speed up old work. They make new work exist.

Start small and start real. Pick one annoying recurring task, the weekly numbers roundup, the price tracking, the “did anything change on that page” check, and agent-ify it. One goal, a few steps, one action at the end. Get it running, watch it work, then make it smarter.

If you want the full map, a friend referred me to a book I have been reading this fall: AI A. The agent architecture patterns, prompt engineering for agents, memory and context management, connecting agents to real-world systems, and 50+ ready-to-use prompts are all in there, and it is the most practical take I have found. Apple Books is featuring it this December in their Great Books, Amazing Deals event, which tells me the timing is right to learn this stuff.

The vending-machine era of AI is over. Time to hire the agent.

Stay in touch. I love to chat about AI; you can find me on LinkedIn.

items.title: Educational Byte: What Are Synthetic Tokens in Crypto Networks?
items.author: Obyte
items.content:
Something “synthetic” is something artificial by nature, a thing that mimics the “real” version. When we add this term to already artificial tokens, it doesn’t mean that these tokens aren’t “real,” but that they follow the price of another asset. It could be from gold, a national currency, a stock, a commodity, another cryptocurrency, or whatever you want.

Still, synthetic tokens aren’t exactly on-chain representations of the referenced asset. If you own a synthetic token that’s tracking the price of gold, this doesn’t give you any ownership of gold itself. It just gives you exposure to the price of the involved asset: If gold rises in price, a synthetic instrument designed to follow it should move in the same direction.

That’s a key difference from (RWAs) tokens, which indeed are a loyal representation of a concrete asset in the real world, not only its general price.

How Do Synthetic Tokens Work?

Smart contracts are at the heart of this type of token. They set the rules for creating, transferring, and managing synthetic positions, while collateral can support those positions. Many systems use overcollateralization, meaning more value is deposited than the value of the synthetic assets created.

is important here because it’s done mainly to manage the risks created by price movements and maintain the synthetic asset's backing. If a synthetic token tracks an asset whose price rises or falls, the collateral needs to provide enough value to support the outstanding synthetic positions. This mechanism creates a buffer between the value of the collateral and the value of the synthetic assets issued, ensuring their existence. are another important piece of the puzzle. To follow prices, you’ll need precise data, and crypto networks don’t have this precise data natively (unless the underlying asset is native to them). That’s why a smart contract for synthetic assets relies on oracles: they’re data feeds that transform external data into on-chain data.

In this case, they bring prices of assets that are completely outside the network, like gold, bonds, or stocks, into the ledger —so the smart contract can read them to calculate values and keep synthetic instruments aligned with their targets.

For a start, a synthetic instrument can provide exposure to an asset or market without requiring the underlying asset itself to move on-chain. That can be useful for commodities, currencies, stocks, and indexes.

They can also interact with decentralized applications (Dapps). Because synthetic assets can exist as on-chain instruments, developers can build them into lending systems, exchanges, automated strategies, or other smart-contract applications. This composability gives financial products more ways to interact with one another instead of sitting in separate systems.

Derivatives are another natural use case. A perpetual future, for instance, can follow the price of an asset while giving traders a tokenized position that doesn't represent ownership of that asset. offer a concrete example. Their tokens follow the prices of currencies, stocks, commodities, or crypto assets using Pythagorean and oracle-provided target prices.

Because these futures are tokens that track external asset prices rather than represent ownership of those assets, they can be considered synthetic assets. The futures never expire, and their price mechanism adjusts toward the target reported by an oracle.

So synthetic tokens cover a broader idea than simply creating a digital copy of something. They turn price exposure into an on-chain, programmable instrument, opening different ways to build financial products around assets that had previously remained outside distributed networks.

items.title: How Timefolk Is Turning Individual Expertise Into Small Group Sessions
items.author: Jon Stojan Journalist
items.content:
Some skills are easier to practise when more than one person is involved. A presentation can benefit from an audience. Language practice becomes more dynamic with several voices in the room. Interview preparation can expose people to different questions and responses.

Timefolk is extending its skills marketplace around that idea. Through, Experts can run small group Events built around a specific skill, with several Clients joining the same practical, in-person session.

The format keeps the same basic structure that sits behind the wider marketplace. The skill, city, session fee and number of available places are clear before someone joins.

In the app, Clients can find an Event through Explore and see the date, skill, fixed session fee, city and remaining spots on the Event card. They can then join and pay through the app. The purpose is established before the group comes together rather than being decided once everyone arrives.

An Expert could run a session around interview practice, Business English, presentation skills, SI tools for work or another practical skill they already use. Several Clients can take part in the same session, creating a different format from an individual session while keeping the activity clearly defined.

For Experts, the group model creates another way to share what they know. Instead of running the same type of session individually with several Clients, an Expert can bring a small group together around one skill. The Expert sets the session fee and the number of available places, while Timefolk provides the marketplace and platform infrastructure around the session.

For Clients, the value is not only the possibility of a lower session fee per person. The group itself can become part of the experience. Someone practising a presentation can receive reactions from more than one participant, while a language session can include different speaking partners. A career focused session can give Clients the opportunity to hear how others approach the same challenge.

The Event still remains tied to one defined skill rather than becoming a general gathering. That distinction is important to Timefolk’s wider positioning as a marketplace for practical, in-person sessions with local Experts.

The platform also keeps the same emphasis on structure. Only ID verified members can join an Event, and every Expert and every Client passes a government ID and liveness check before a session. The exact place is provided before the Event, and the venue must be public. Timefolk’s current product material excludes homes, bars and private rooms from the Event format. Timefolk-media-deck

The session begins through an Event code or QR, creating a clear point at which attendance is recorded. Timefolk also states that only people who attended can leave a review. Timefolk-media-deck

Payments are handled through the app, with Clients able to use methods including Apple Pay, Google Pay or a saved card. Timefolk’s broader payment infrastructure uses Stripe. Timefolk-media-deck

The company has also built specific features around the group format. Its current media deck describes a shared Event page, a QR image that Experts can use when promoting the session, a list showing who attended and tools for managing the Event inside the platform. Clients can receive a full refund if an Event is cancelled or if they leave at least 24 hours before it starts. If the time or place changes, the platform provides a window for Clients to leave without charge. Timefolk-media-deck

Those details matter because group sessions create different operational questions from individual sessions. The platform needs to show who has joined, how many places remain, what happens if the venue changes and how attendance is confirmed.

Timefolk is trying to answer those questions inside the product rather than leaving them to informal coordination. That makes Events more than simply an additional format. They show how a skills marketplace can expand without losing the structure that defines the original model.

One Expert can offer a practical skill to several Clients while the purpose, session fee, location and participation rules remain visible from the beginning.

For Timefolk, that creates another way for expertise to move through a city. A practical skill no longer has to be shared with one Client at a time. It can become a small group session built around the same clear outcome.

items.title: I Put My Country's Entire Legal Code in Git: 300,000+ Documents Since 1810
items.author: Maximiliano Morel
items.content:
This article explains how I built a Git repository of Chile's entire legal code: more than 300,000 laws, decrees and resolutions in a corpus that reaches back to 1810, with one commit per legislative publication, so the text of any law can be read as it stood on any date. It covers scraping the Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional (BCN) and LeyChile, building the history with git fast-import, the limits of Git and GitHub that the repository hit, and the web UI, API and MCP server built on top of it. The repository is pisanvs/ley-chile, and you can browse it at leyes.pisanvs.cl.

Why Version Control for Legislation?

I think most programmers would agree that working—in a team—without a version control system like Git, is as horrifying as ripping your nails out with bare hands. Git has become a ubiquitous tool in the software industry, not because it’s amazing, but because it’s undoubtedly necessary.

As coders and hackers, we tend to believe in the delusion that we can fix others’ problems by working our fingers against the keyboard. This is partly (mostly) the reason why one of my obsessions is making other fields of work more efficient.

One of these fields of work is law. You see, the lawyers I know religiously use either Google Docs’ or MS Word’s implementations of version control systems. This doesn’t look like a bad idea or use-case at first glance, but upon further examination we can see the shortcomings of this approach.

🚧 (“blame” doesn’t exist, you must rely on version history)

❌ (need to create a separate file)

Intentional & Directed commits

❌ “versions” are just point-in-time objects

✅ Can stage specific hunks, write commit messages, explain changes.

Selective historical undo

❌ Can only revert to a specific version

Now, we programmers use these features regularly, but other fields of work don’t. They don’t have the tools and they have to find increasingly complex workarounds.

A good place to start the Git crusade, in my opinion, is the law.

Existing Git Repositories of Laws: US Code and Legalize

There are some projects around the world that have tried doing this to varying levels of success.

nickvido’s us-code repository on GitHub has one substantial shortcoming: it only has 16 commits.

How many bills have been passed to modify laws in the US Code? Thousands. At least a few hundred per two-year congressional term. But this doesn’t check out. Why? Because this repo is built from the point-in-time snapshots from the Library of Congress, instead of having its history built per bill.

In my humble opinion, although this repo is accurate, it does not provide a value-add over what the Library of Congress snapshots already provide.

Legalize is probably the most complete solution that has scaled this up to multiple countries. But sadly, their Chilean repo is a bit behind: it only has 3k laws and reforms in it, compared to the more than 300k norms in the complete Chilean corpus.

I really appreciate the work Legalize has done. If I had been aware of their existence before I started this project, I probably would’ve made a fork instead of starting from scratch.

Requirements for a Git-Based Legal Code Repository

Apart from being mostly unaware of other solutions, the reason I built this project this way was because I had some very particular requirements and constraints. No good engineering challenge has few constraints, after all!

Some of these requirements are considered (rightfully so) a bit outrageous by some friends of mine. I would agree for the most part!

  1. It must fully live within Git
  2. The code should be as simple and compact as possible
  3. Maintainers need not worry about updates to the law

The main purpose of these requirements is to have an easily clone-able, replicable and iterable source for the data and the scraper/generator alike. This enables some benefits of distribution and accessibility, which the traditional sources don’t have.

A fourth bonus requirement was to have the pipeline run alongside the repo. The default option for this was of course GitHub Actions. Having a self-contained GitHub repository for the whole “ecosystem” makes it easy for anyone to clone, modify, and distribute as needed.

Now, having this pipeline run completely within GitHub actions generates its own set of weird constraints. Contrary to popular belief, it has actually brought on some benefits, especially related to the fact that public facing IPs on each job tend to be distinct, and thus lets you circumvent some rate limiters by spreading your work across IPs.

Chilean Legal Data Sources: BCN, LeyChile and SPARQL

Lucky for the Chilean folk, our National Library of Congress keeps in-depth, updated, accurate and densely linked data on the legal history of the country. They’ve got laws spanning from the country’s first provisional government in 1810 to the present day. The founding act of the First Government Junta is dated 18 September 1810, the day Chile now celebrates as its national day. The Acta de la Instalación de la Primera Junta de Gobierno is one example from the beginning of the corpus.

Another early entry shows how broad the words “legal code” are in the Library. They file “Medidas contra la sífilis” as a decree, but it’s really a letter from the government to a marquis, dated 13 January 1813. Providence, they say, put the cure to syphilis in the hot springs on the marquis’ estate, and the government would like the sick to be able to reach them. So it asks him what road work is needed between Rancagua and the baths, and how it could be paid for. It is an early example of a government text with practical force, even though it might look like it’s very informal.

The Chilean Library of Congress, BCN from now on, exposes multiple APIs, to the point where it’s not possible to have a single source that trumps the rest.

The first two APIs are used and each serves a specific purpose in this project. The only API that is not being used is the API-key-restricted one.

the SPARQL endpoint, is the fastest way to get the list of everything that exists on the server. With one query we can get every norm's leychileCode, type and publication date. Unfortunately, the server times out on deep OFFSETs, so the script pages with a keyset cursor asking for 500 sequential codes at a time.

curl https://datos.bcn.cl/sparql \
  --data-urlencode 'format=application/json' \
  --data-urlencode 'query=
PREFIX bcn: <http://datos.bcn.cl/ontologies/bcn-norms#>
PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#>
SELECT DISTINCT ?code ?tipo ?date WHERE {
  ?s bcn:leychileCode ?code .
  FILTER(xsd:integer(?code) > 0)
  OPTIONAL { ?s bcn:type ?t . BIND(STR(?t) AS ?tipo) }
  OPTIONAL { ?s bcn:publishDate ?date }
}
ORDER BY xsd:integer(?code)
LIMIT 500'

This query is from our first stage of the process, which is building the catalog.

the norm JSON, gives me all data corresponding to one norm, and the text of any version of it. The same endpoint serves both the metadata and the versioned text. The difference is one parameter:

# metadata and current text of a norm
curl 'https://nuevo.leychile.cl/servicios/Navegar/get_norma_json?idNorma=<ID>'

# the same norm as it read on a given date
curl 'https://nuevo.leychile.cl/servicios/Navegar/get_norma_json?idNorma=<ID>&idVersion=2009-04-01&agrupa_partes=1'

The response is an HTML-like tree with law fragments plus a list of the dated versions the norm has had. Inside the HTML are callouts with links to the norms that modified it, and that's where I get the edges of the graph (more on that in the next section).

The third API, bcn.cl/leychile/api/v1, I never used. It needs an API key, and the quota is 500 requests per day per key. At 358,000 norms, one pass would take about two years of quota, before counting any versions. This is a separate issue, but when scraping doesn’t affect in a negative way the infrastructure of a service, and the second best way to get the data is actively harmful for performance or results, it’s probably a symptom of a system that isn’t really open, independent of how much the orgs publicize the “open data” aspect of it.

Scraping Chilean Laws from LeyChile and the BCN from GitHub Actions

Ingesting all of this data is an interesting task. It is weirdly shaped, not always complete, or accurate, or standardized.

The scraper is, in essence, four idempotent scripts that run in order.

  1. pages through SPARQL and writes catalog.json, the list of every norm ID, its type and its publication date.
  2. downloads each norm's metadata into graph.json. For every norm it pulls the links out of the HTML tree, and each link to another norm becomes an edge: "this norm was modified by that one". The result is the amendment graph of the whole legal system.
  3. downloads every dated version of every norm and computes the diffs between them.
  4. turns the cache into Git commits.

A note on counts, since they appear throughout: in the main branch’s builder, the catalog contained about 358,000 norms. Roughly 19,000 lacked a usable publication date or had only sentinel dates, leaving about 339,000 that this builder could place in history. Those are pipeline figures, not a count of what the deployed site can show; its Railway deployment uses a different path. The search index in a later section was loaded when it stood at 333,026 norms.

SPARQL ─► catalog.json ─► get_norma_json ─► graph.json (amendment edges)
                                     │
                                     ▼
                       get_norma_json?idVersion=… ─► cache/versions + cache/diffs
                                     │
                                     ▼
                      git fast-import stream ─► branch historial

Now, trying to scrape data means that it’s probably going to fight back the whole way. Some of these examples are the following.

  • The endpoint is behind a flaky firewall: My first runs on GitHub Actions came back with Expecting value: line 1 column 1. I assumed those were dead IDs. They weren't. From my home connection, every URL in the failure log returned valid JSON. From a GitHub runner (Azure IPs), the WAF answered with HTTP 200 and a 264-byte block page. The fix was to send a full Chrome-style header set.
  • A missing norm sometimes also returns 200 with an empty body, and a few return 500 with a “not found” message. These looked identical to WAF blocks, so dead IDs were being retried forever and throttling the whole crawl. Now both are marked permanent after one failure and don't count as a load signal.
  • My rate limiter deadlocked. A run with 16,629 tasks went silent for two hours right after the first resize from 3 to 4 parallel slots. The fix was to change the live semaphore instead of replacing it.
  • 358,000 tasks at once is a bad idea for GitHub actions (lol) Implementing parallel task scheduling was key to unlock better performance.
  • We restored catalog.json with cp, which resets the file's modification time on every run. The "is the catalog stale?" check read the mtime, so the catalog always looked brand new and was never refreshed. The fix was to stamp a fetched_at timestamp inside the file and read the age from that, and to make CI warn if the newest data is more than seven days behind.

Because every stage can be resumed, the work gets spread across GitHub Action runs. The pipeline runs every 3 hours in three phases. A first job refreshes the catalog and graph when they're more than a day old. Then the version fetch runs on 8 parallel runners to avoid IP rate-limiting, since each runner gets a different IP. The last job merges the eight shard branches back into pipeline-cache, rebuilds historial, and pushes it. A concurrency group makes sure only one run can write historial at a time.

Git Repository Size Limits: When a Legal Code Breaks Git

An average library, with 10,000 books, should store around 20 GB of just text. There’s a reason why we have a Library of Congress.

The ley-chile repo stores almost 20 GB of pure normative text.

At this scale, some things start to break.

To some extent, the ley-chile repo has broken two of these limits: the size of its tree objects and the width of its directories.

git cat-file --batch-all-objects --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectsize)' | awk '{s[$1]+=$2; t+=$2} END {for(k in s) printf "%s %.2f GiB\n",k,s[k]/2^30; printf "total %.2f GiB\n",t/2^30}'

commit 0.12 GiB
tree 375.27 GiB
blob 17.24 GiB
total 392.63 GiB

This is the uncompressed size of the repo. Note that the on-disk value is much smaller:

What this means is that if you were to count every version of every file ever committed, you would have around 17 GiB of data in total (blobs). You can see that the trees take up the most space. Why is this?

Git never edits objects in place. When you change one file, Git writes a new blob for it. Then it writes a new tree for every directory on the path from that file up to the root, because each parent's listing now holds a new hash.

For a normal repo that costs little. Here, directories like cache/versions/ or leyes/ list thousands of entries each. Every commit that touches even one law rewrites those huge listings in full. Thousands of commits * multi-MB listings = 375 GiB uncompressed.

Which leads us to the second limit broken: directory width. The three biggest folders in the repo are all inside the pipeline-cache branch (an orphan branch that holds the downloaded data; the rebuilt history of the laws lives in a second orphan branch, historial, described below). They all have more than 357k entries.

In the history branch, with the “rendered” repository, you will see the biggest folder by entries is etc/res with all of the resolutions from different state organisms.

A few more things that broke or had me bang my head against a wall along the way:

  • Two resolutions with the same number in one folder. Res N°20, from the “Municipalidad de Tocopilla” and Res N°20, from the DGA, both wrote to etc/res/20/. The second one silently overwrote the first with no notice. I fixed this with a forward-pass over the whole 357,000-node graph that hands out paths in ID order, so the first norm keeps etc/res/20/ and the second becomes etc/res/20-1163150/.
  • A helper returned ley for an empty type, so every untyped norm landed in leyes/. A related bug dropped any law with no number into leyes/ with identical names, and they all overwrote each other's metadata.json. Unknown types now go to etc/unknown/<id>/, and number-less laws are filed by ID.
  • GitHub's 100 MB blob limit. At some point, pushes of pipeline-cache started being rejected because the diffs of three large codes were over the limit: norm 6368 at 100.11 MB, 8201 at 117 MB and 207436 at 137 MB. They're HTML-heavy, so gzip shrank them about tenfold (76 MB down to 7.6 MB), and the cache now stores .json.gz.
  • Git's default http.postBuffer is 1 MB. Above that it switches to chunked transfer encoding, which GitHub's endpoint often rejects for big packs. I raised the buffer to 2 GB and cut the chunk size from 500 commits to 100, since 500 commits of multi-MB texto.md files made 1–2 GB packs. Then I found that git push can exit 0 with "Everything up-to-date" a mid-stream disconnect, so the script now checks with git ls-remote that the branch actually moved and retries up to 5 times.
  • The runner ran out of disk. The pipeline-cache worktree has around 1.1 million files. A run died at 92% of the checkout with "No space left on device" on a runner with about 14 GB free. I ended up using an action template to delete the runner's preinstalled Android SDK and .NET toolchains (about 30 GB), and on top of that, used a sparse checkout that skips the per-norm metadata folder.

Git History: One Commit per Publication

The useful unit of history is a publication, not a law or an edit within a single file. A new Chilean norm can amend several older ones at once, so I made each publication a single commit containing the new norm and every change it caused. Open that commit and you can see the legal change as one event.

I wrote about the mechanics of generating those commits with in my previous article. Here, that commit model matters because it powers the diffs and historical lookups below.

The full story, with the code, is in my previous article as well. Three things shaped this project:

  • Git can't hold a date before 1970 in a repo that GitHub will accept. (The failures, as I showed in my previous article: --date silently falls back to the current year, the environment variables give a misleading "invalid date format", and fsck rejects what fast-import lets through.) GitHub runs git fsck --strict on every push, and negative timestamps fail it. In the main pipeline, my fix collapses every pre-1970 commit into the first few seconds of 1970, one second apart so they still sort in order, and keeps the real date in two places Git doesn't police: the metadata.json stored next to each law (fechaPublicacion), and the commit subject as publicada (YYYY-MM-DD) for every amendment. The main pipeline’s index builder reads the date from the subject, not from Git's own timestamp.
  • Same-day collisions. Commit timestamps have to be unique, so publications that share a day are shifted by a second. At one point this also moved some real post-1970 dates by a day. Reading the date from the subject fixed that too.
  • Past 2099, Git's --date parsing fails, while raw timestamps keep working. This hasn't hit the project, because I filter anything above 2100 as the 2222-02-02 sentinel.

I also tried the alternatives for the dates, as I described in my previous article. Mercurial accepts 1901 through 2038, which is a bit wider than Git for the past but closes the future sooner. Fossil stores dates as Julian day numbers in SQLite, so it took every date in the corpus, including early nineteenth-century dates.

Web UI, API and MCP Server for Searching Chilean Law

For our users to actually make good use of the data, we needed to expose it in a more familiar interface. Given Git’s and GitHub’s constraints, the fact that the existing GitHub UI wasn’t made for exploring data of this shape, and the hard limits around datetimes, metadata, linking, etc, I decided to go forward building a Web UI for the project. This was probably the best decision I made.

The web UI makes it easy for lawyers and regular users to take advantage of Git’s utility, while not necessarily having to interact with it. Common interactions are implemented, with Git-specific functionality available for power users who are willing to clone the repo.

A counterpart of the Web UI is an API and an MCP server. These can get quick access to the corpus with the main functionality being search. Search is a big challenge, especially when storing not only the latest versions but also the full history.

The directory structure of ley-chile only serves quick lookup when the user previously knows the text’s type and id. For any semantic search, another layer is needed. Just grep-ing over the whole directory is an immensely slow operation. The challenge then becomes building a search engine over the corpus.

The site started with two search tiers. Meilisearch stored the top ~8% of laws that people actually read, 28,730 of 333,026, and Postgres held the rest. This was supposed to be an 80/20 solution to the search problem, but it actually became very expensive!

Postgres full-text index on articles (articulo_tsv_idx)

That is about sixteen times the disk for under a tenth of the content. There was a second cost in memory. Meilisearch memory-maps its index, so its resident memory climbs to cover the working set and never comes back down, and Railway bills observed memory, so the mapped index was a continuous charge. A premium price to pay even with no usage being registered.

What settled it was an outage. On 2026-09-07 Meilisearch didn't come back from a Railway region migration. Search returned nothing for every query, including a bare law number that Postgres could have answered, because the code awaited the Meilisearch tier unconditionally and swallowed the error. A dependency serving under a tenth of the corpus took down 100% of search, and did it with a 200 response and an empty list.

So I moved all of it into Postgres, in two parts:

  • works at the level of a whole norm, not article text. A table of about 333,000 rows holds the title, the common names people use ("ley de partidos") and the number, with a small text-search function over it. Ranking is by type (laws and codes outrank decrees and resolutions, because "1" alone matches around 450 decrees), by how often the law has been amended, and by how often people look it up. Typeahead takes about 3 ms.
  • over article text has two query shapes whose benefits measurably balance each other. For a common word like "trabajo", walking the norms in ID order finds 20 matches in about 2.5 ms. That same shape on a rare word never finds 20 and degenerates into a full table scan. The other shape ranks everything through the full-text index first, which is fast for a rare word and slow for a common one. The deep search function estimates how many articles will match from a table of word frequencies, and picks the shape. The crossover sits near the square root of the corpus size, so the threshold is computed when data loads (it resolved to 1,868).

"geotermia" (149 matches)

"contrato" (60,644 matches)

The old query took 21 seconds because Postgres chose the wrong index and removed 524,720 rows by filter while never touching the full-text index at all. Making one query shape the default would have made common words 38 times slower, this justifies the logical overhead.

This was the point when I removed the Meilisearch client and its volume. It's not perfect. When a common word has thousands of matches, the fast shape picks which 20 laws to show by lowest ID, not by relevance. This probably justifies the decision to build a different engine at some point, but with an LLM in front of the search, as with the MCP server, it works well enough most of the time.

The fact that we had to build all of this separate infrastructure on top goes to show how Git really isn’t the best format to store this type of data. But alas, it is very useful for a specific purpose.

Use Cases: Legal History, Law Diffs and AI Agents

  • "What changed, word for word, between these two points in time?" - Creating diffs is easy in Git. The web UI has a redline view that compares two versions of a law, with deletions in red and additions in green. The diff_versions tool does the same for agents.
  • "What touches this law?" - The data is structured such that a single commit will show this. Amended laws arrive along with their reform texts. In the MCP get_modifications lists the norms that amended a law and the ones it amends. It’s very useful for understanding the evolution of legislation around a topic.
  • A JSON API for developers. https://leyes.pisanvs.cl/api/v1 has search, norm metadata and article endpoints, an OpenAPI 3.1 spec at /api/v1/openapi.json (the docs page is at /api), and an asOf=YYYY-MM-DD parameter that searches the text in force on that date. Keys are issued by hand. Here's a search for "partidos politicos":
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $LEYCHILE_KEY" \
  'https://leyes.pisanvs.cl/api/v1/search?q=partidos+politicos&limit=2'

The first result is idNorma 29994, "Ley Orgánica Constitucional de los Partidos Políticos" (Ley 18603). Note that every endpoint takes an idNorma, not a type and number. (tipo, numero) doesn't identify a Chilean norm: there are 227 “DFL 1”, 75 “DFL 4” and 525 “DTO 1”. At one point the endpoint for law 20780 /ley/20780 resolved to an unrelated decree whose internal ID happened to be 20780.

  • There is a read-only MCP server at https://leyes.pisanvs.cl/api/mcp, with no authentication and eight tools: search_laws, get_law, get_article, search_articles, diff_versions, get_modifications, list_versions and get_raw_link. To add it to Claude Code:
claude mcp add --transport http ley-chile https://leyes.pisanvs.cl/api/mcp

There's also a /llms.txt with instructions written for agents. This is how most users discover this project, and is probably the most useful use case that impacts efficiency.

Should You Put Legislation in Git?

, if you care about the text of the law being traceable. A Git history gives you something a PDF can't: every version has a hash, every change has a cause, and "the law as of date X" is a command instead of a research project. Lawyers don't need better word processors for this. They need blame, diff and log, which they have never had.

You shouldn't expect Git to be the product. My lawyer friends will keep using Word. What made the project usable for them was the web UI on top, so Git ended up as the engine and not the interface. And it's not even a good database: search needed Postgres, and my first search engine (Meilisearch) cost about 16 times the disk for under a tenth of the corpus and took search down with it when it went offline. In the final design Git is the single source of truth, and everything else (Postgres, the search tables) is derived and can be thrown away and rebuilt. Right now, the MCP seems to be the biggest product.

You should check the limits before you start. GitHub caps blobs at 100 MB, rejects pushes with big packs, and runs fsck on everything you send it. Read the repository limits first. I learned most of them from rejected pushes.

items.title: OpenAI Might Rebrand Its Data Centers As 'AI Compute Campuses'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a "PR blitz" for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too. The company's chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be "a bit of a movie trailer for what you're going to see in 2028," when he expects AI to be "the issue" in the presidential election.
 
So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI "speed limits"; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards; and yes -- rebranding data centers as "AI compute campuses." Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments) as "good and healthy." "Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects," he said.

items.title: Guardz Integrates Palo Alto Networks Prisma Browser Protection to Address Growing Workspace Security
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
The browser has become one of the most important tools in the modern workplace. Employees use it to access business applications, communicate with colleagues, manage sensitive information, and increasingly interact with generative AI platforms. As more business activity moves into browser-based environments, the security risks associated with these interactions are becoming harder to manage through traditional endpoint and email protection alone.

A phishing email, for example, may appear to be an isolated threat. But when an employee follows a malicious link, the consequences can extend to compromised credentials,, unauthorized access to cloud applications, and potentially an exposed endpoint. Understanding the full scope of such an incident requires security teams to connect activity across multiple parts of the workplace.

As shared with this writer through a press release, is addressing this challenge through a new integration with Palo Alto Networks, bringing browser-level protection to its security platform.

Guardz, a cybersecurity platform built for managed service providers (MSPs), has announced the integration of from Palo Alto Networks. The integration brings browser protection into Guardz's broader security environment, connecting browser activity with signals from email, identity, endpoints, data, and user risk.

The objective is to give MSPs and security teams a more connected view of threats affecting the organizations they protect, particularly small businesses that may lack dedicated security operations resources.

Through the integration, Prisma Browser for Business can block malicious websites, including fraudulent login pages designed to capture employee credentials. Guardz can then correlate the browser event with the original phishing email, related Microsoft 365 activity, and endpoint telemetry.

Rather than treating each signal as an independent security alert, the platform can bring the associated activity together to support investigation and response as a unified incident.

For Guardz CEO and Co-Founder Dor Eisner, this approach reflects a broader change in how organizations should think about cybersecurity.

“Identity is the new center of gravity in cybersecurity, and the browser has become the primary gateway to the modern workspace. Traditional security tools operate in silos, leaving critical gaps in visibility and response,” Eisner said.

Moving Beyond Isolated Security Alerts

The integration introduces several browser security capabilities into the Guardz environment.

Prisma Browser for Business uses inline machine-learning phishing detection and to help identify and block malicious websites. This includes pages designed to impersonate legitimate services and attacks intended to steal active session tokens.

The integration also incorporates to help detect malicious files, alongside browser security scanning for uploads and downloads. Risky browser extensions can also be identified, addressing another potential entry point for attackers.

These capabilities become particularly relevant when considered alongside the wider incident investigation process.

If an employee encounters a malicious login page, browser protection can prevent access to the site. Guardz can then connect that event to other activity involving the same identity, giving the MSP and Guardz's 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) team additional context for determining whether the incident extends beyond the initial click.

Eisner described the broader objective as connecting security signals through an identity-centered architecture.

“Together with Palo Alto Networks, we’re advancing a new era of identity-centric security operations, connecting signals across identity, browser, email, endpoint, and data into a unified security fabric that is powered by agents. Guardz enables MSPs to autonomously investigate, correlate, and respond to threats across the entire workspace, while giving small businesses the freedom to embrace AI securely and thrive. This is the future of cybersecurity: identity-centric, unified data fabric, and built for autonomous defense at scale,” Eisner added.

Making Browser Security Easier To Deploy

For MSPs, security technology must also be practical to implement across multiple customer environments. Complex deployment requirements can make otherwise useful tools difficult to introduce, particularly when supporting organizations with limited IT resources.

Guardz says its integration streamlines provisioning, setup, and default configuration, allowing MSPs to deploy browser protection within minutes once the required tenant approvals are completed.

Early-access feedback from Datawise Networks highlighted the deployment experience. Kevin Kehoe of Datawise Networks said, “The rollout through our RMM was super smooth. Within minutes, the Prisma Browser for Business extension was on every Chrome and Edge profile, and it was quick and easy to configure and deploy.”

The simplified deployment process is designed to help MSPs extend browser security across their customer environments without introducing unnecessary operational overhead.

Preparing Small Businesses For A Browser-Driven Workplace

The announcement also addresses the growing use of browser-based AI tools. As employees increasingly turn to generative AI services for everyday work, organizations need visibility into which platforms are being used and how company information is being shared.

Guardz's AI Usage and Control capabilities allow technicians to establish client-specific policies governing activities such as copying, pasting, uploading, and downloading files. Restrictions can be applied by website or category.

The company has also introduced an AI usage report that gives MSPs a per-client view of AI tool adoption based on available security signals.

Shivam Srivastava, VP Product at Palo Alto Networks, sees the collaboration as an opportunity to bring browser protection to organizations that may not otherwise have access to the same level of security coverage.

“For most small businesses, the browser is now the office. Working with Guardz brings Prisma Browser for Business into the security these organizations receive from the providers they already trust. It connects our browser protection with the wider coverage and support their MSP delivers, helping safeguard the applications and information employees use every day,” Srivastava said.

As business applications and AI tools increasingly operate through browsers, securing that environment is becoming a more central part of protecting the modern workplace. Guardz's integration with Palo Alto Networks reflects an effort to bring browser activity into the wider security picture rather than leaving it as another isolated source of risk.
