items.title: Making Local LLMs Usable on 8GB GPUs
items.author: Naresh Waghela
items.content:
A local model can manage a brief question without any issues, but it may have difficulty when dealing with a complete document. The model's internal settings stay the same, but the effort needed and the memory required to process the request increase a lot.

In , I explained how to run a quantized model on a smaller GPU.

The next step is to choose a task, measure how long it takes, and find a setup that works within the GPU's limits.

This guide uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct along with llama.cpp.

It includes memory calculations, a fixed starting configuration, and a Python-based benchmark that you can run on your own computer. The numerical memory estimates are calculated values, and this article does not claim to have measured improvements in GPU performance.

To understand the actual delay you experience, there are two main waiting periods in a conversation. The first occurs when the model processes the initial prompt, often called the prefill phase. The second happens when the model generates the answer one word at a time, known as the decode phase.

If a document takes several seconds to process, fast decoding won't eliminate that initial delay. However, if the first words appear quickly but the rest of the response is slow, then the decoding phase is the area that needs optimization.

Keep these measurements separate:

A target such as "start a short answer within two seconds" can guide your own experiments. It is a product requirement you choose, not a promised result for every 8GB card.

Budget for the KV cache as well as the weights

The model file is only part of the memory requirement. During generation, the runtime also stores attention keys and values for tokens already processed. This avoids recomputing those states, but it needs memory of its own. Working buffers and other GPU applications need space too. [1]

For a conventional full-attention transformer, an approximate KV-cache payload is:

KV bytes = 2 x layers x stored tokens x KV heads x head dimension

x bytes per cache element

The initial 2 accounts for keys and values. Use the number of , which can differ from the number of query heads.

Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct has 28 layers, 4 KV heads, and a head dimension of 128, obtained from its hidden size of 3,584 divided by 28 query heads. With FP16 cache elements, the calculation becomes 2 x 28 x tokens x 4 x 128 x 2. [2]

These figures describe one sequence and exclude allocation padding, runtime buffers, and model weights. They are not measurements of total VRAM usage. Other architectures, cache layouts, and attention types need different calculations.

This is why a large advertised context window needs its own memory budget. On this model, moving from 4K to 32K tokens adds about 1.53 GiB of calculated FP16 cache payload. Whether that increase fits depends on everything else already occupying the GPU.

Weight quantization and cache quantization are separate choices. A Q4_K_M model can still use an FP16 KV cache. Reducing cache precision may free up space, but it needs a quality check and a latency measurement. Hugging Face's cache documentation also cautions that cache quantization can hurt latency in some short-context situations. [1]

Establish one repeatable baseline

The shell commands below target Linux or WSL2 with an NVIDIA GPU. Install a working NVIDIA driver, a compatible CUDA Toolkit, Git, CMake, and a C++ compiler first. The benchmark itself requires Python 3.10 or newer and no third-party Python packages.

Use the current CMake build route in the llama.cpp build documentation: [3]

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --config Release -j 4
git rev-parse HEAD > llama-commit.txt
./build/bin/llama-server --version > llama-version.txt
./build/bin/llama-server --help > llama-help.txt
nvidia-smi > gpu-environment.txt

Keep that checkout unchanged throughout the experiment. Save the model filenames and their SHA-256 hashes too, including every shard if the download is split. A model tag alone is not enough to reproduce an experiment after its files change.

I use the official Qwen GGUF repository because its model configuration is available to inspect. It is a concrete baseline, not a claim that this is the best available model. [4]

Start the server from the llama.cpp directory:

./build/bin/llama-server \
  -hf Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-GGUF:Q4_K_M \
  --n-gpu-layers all \
  --ctx-size 4096 --parallel 1 \
  --batch-size 512 --ubatch-size 128 \
  --flash-attn off \
  --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 \
  --fit off --no-context-shift --perf \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 \
  2> baseline-server.log

The first launch downloads the selected model. Exclude that download and startup from request timings. Once the server is ready, inspect its log for the CUDA device, layer placement, cache allocation, and effective context settings. If an installed version rejects an option, consult its saved help output before continuing. The current server options are documented upstream. [5]

This configuration requests full GPU offload; it does not guarantee that every 8GB system has enough free memory. If startup fails, first close another GPU workload or test a smaller context. If partial offload is necessary, record the actual GPU layer count and use it consistently across the comparison.

The baseline has one request slot. Keep other inference clients stopped while measuring. With automatic fitting disabled, a failed configuration is visible instead of becoming a different experiment through an adjusted setting.

Run a benchmark that preserves the evidence

Save this small input as prompt.txt:

Answer using only these project notes.

Project Cedar: Mira owns the CSV import validator.

The release target is 15 November 2026.

Duplicate IDs are blocking the import test.

No project budget has been approved.

In at most 80 words, identify the owner, target date, and blocker. Then say whether the notes contain an approved budget amount. Do not invent missing details. Save the following script as bench_local.py. It formats the prompt using the server's chat template, checks a declared token budget, performs a warm-up, and records five measured requests by default.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Measure a local llama-server with Python 3.10+ standard libraries only."""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
import statistics
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen
 
 
def request(base, route, data):
    body = json.dumps(data).encode("utf-8")
    return Request(base + route, data=body,
                   headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
 
 
def post(base, route, data):
    with urlopen(request(base, route, data), timeout=120) as response:
        value = json.load(response)
    if "error" in value:
        raise RuntimeError(str(value["error"]))
    return value
 
 
def events(response):
    """Parse complete SSE events, including multiple data lines."""
    data = []
    for raw in response:
        line = raw.decode("utf-8").rstrip("\r\n")
        if not line:
            if data:
                payload = "\n".join(data)
                if payload == "[DONE]":
                    return
                yield json.loads(payload)
                data = []
        elif line.startswith("data:"):
            data.append(line[5:].removeprefix(" "))
    if data:
        raise RuntimeError("Incomplete SSE event at end of stream")
 
 
def measure(base, prompt, max_tokens):
    req = request(base, "/completion", {
        "prompt": prompt, "stream": True, "n_predict": max_tokens,
        "temperature": 0, "seed": 42, "cache_prompt": False,
    })
    first = final = None
    parts = []
    started = time.perf_counter()
    with urlopen(req, timeout=300) as response:
        for event in events(response):
            if "error" in event:
                raise RuntimeError(str(event["error"]))
            content = event.get("content", "")
            if content:
                if first is None:
                    first = time.perf_counter() - started
                parts.append(content)
            if event.get("stop"):
                final = event
                break
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
    if final is None:
        raise RuntimeError("Stream ended without final completion statistics")
    if final.get("truncated"):
        raise RuntimeError("Context overflow invalidated this run")
    timing = final.get("timings", {})
    needed = ("prompt_n", "prompt_ms", "predicted_n", "predicted_per_second")
    if any(key not in timing for key in needed):
        raise RuntimeError("Missing timings; check --perf and server version")
    if timing.get("cache_n", 0):
        raise RuntimeError("Unexpected prefix-cache reuse invalidated this run")
    if first is None or timing["predicted_n"] <= 0:
        raise RuntimeError("No generated text to measure")
    return {
        "ttft_s": first, "elapsed_s": elapsed,
        "decode_tok_s": timing["predicted_per_second"],
        "prompt_tokens": timing["prompt_n"],
        "prompt_eval_ms": timing["prompt_ms"],
        "output_tokens": timing["predicted_n"],
        "cached_prompt_tokens": timing.get("cache_n"),
        "stop_type": final.get("stop_type"),
        "text": "".join(parts),
    }
 
 
def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--prompt", type=Path, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--label", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--base", default="http://127.0.0.1:8080")
    parser.add_argument("--context", type=int, default=4096)
    parser.add_argument("--max-tokens", type=int, default=256)
    parser.add_argument("--runs", type=int, default=5)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if min(args.context, args.max_tokens, args.runs) <= 0:
        parser.error("context, max-tokens and runs must be positive")
    base = args.base.rstrip("/")
    user_text = args.prompt.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_text}]
    prompt = post(base, "/apply-template", {"messages": messages})["prompt"]
    tokens = post(base, "/tokenize", {
        "content": prompt, "add_special": True, "parse_special": True,
    })["tokens"]
    if len(tokens) + args.max_tokens + 32 > args.context:
        parser.error("prompt + output + 32-token reserve exceeds --context")
    warmup = measure(base, prompt, args.max_tokens)
    runs = [measure(base, prompt, args.max_tokens) for _ in range(args.runs)]
    metrics = ("ttft_s", "elapsed_s", "decode_tok_s")
    report = {
        "label": args.label, "base": base,
        "prompt_sha256": hashlib.sha256(user_text.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "formatted_prompt_tokens": len(tokens),
        "declared_context": args.context, "max_tokens": args.max_tokens,
        "cache_prompt": False, "warmup": warmup, "runs": runs,
        "median": {key: statistics.median(r[key] for r in runs)
                   for key in metrics},
        "range": {key: [min(r[key] for r in runs), max(r[key] for r in runs)]
                  for key in metrics},
    }
    print(json.dumps(report, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))
 
 
if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except HTTPError as exc:
        detail = exc.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
        raise SystemExit(f"HTTP {exc.code}: {detail}") from exc
    except (URLError, OSError, ValueError, KeyError, RuntimeError) as exc:
        raise SystemExit(f"Benchmark failed: {exc}") from exc

In a second terminal, run it from the folder containing the script and input:

python3 bench_local.py --prompt prompt.txt \
  --label A-4096-F16 --context 4096 > A-short.json

Its is a client-side approximation of time to first token: timing starts before the generation HTTP request and stops at the first nonempty content chunk. That chunk may contain more than one token. Template formatting, token counting, model loading, and any document retrieval happen outside this timer.

The script uses the server's token statistics for decoding speed. Counting streaming events would measure chunks, whose boundaries are not reliable token boundaries. The native completion endpoint and its timing fields are documented in llama.cpp. [5]

Prefix reuse is disabled for these comparisons. The model still uses a KV cache within each generation; the setting prevents an identical prompt from being accelerated by a previous request's prefix. The separate warm-up is excluded from the median. Failed or truncated requests stop the experiment instead of producing a successful-looking score.

The --context value is a declared budget, not a command that reconfigures the server. Match it to the server's effective context. The script allows an additional 32-token reserve and records the formatted input token count.

Repeat the test with a realistic document saved in another input file. Keep that file unchanged across configurations. A short fixture helps check the pipeline, but it cannot establish long-document performance.

Change one setting at a time

Restart the server for each configuration, adjusting only the settings listed here. Everything else, including weights, prompt files, output cap, and GPU placement, stays fixed.

A to B tests Flash Attention. B to C tests cache precision. C to D tests the larger context allocation. D to E tests a larger physical batch. Q8_0 cache support depends on the model, backend, and build; inspect startup output and skip unsupported combinations rather than comparing a fallback unknowingly. [5]

For C, replace the baseline attention and cache options with:

--flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0

Flash Attention is designed to reduce memory traffic during attention computation. It does not remove the persistent KV-cache requirement. [6] A larger physical batch may help prompt processing but can require more temporary memory, so treat E as an experiment rather than a recommended default.

There are two different comparisons to make. Use the across A through E to compare configuration overhead. Separately, increase the actual input length to study longer requests. Changing an 8K capacity setting while keeping a 200-token prompt does not simulate an 8K prompt.

Monitor GPU usage in a third terminal: [7]

nvidia-smi \
  --query-gpu=timestamp,name,memory.total,memory.used,utilization.gpu \
  --format=csv -l 1 > gpu-samples.csv

Stop sampling with Ctrl+C when the experiment ends. These are device-wide samples, including other processes; one-second sampling can miss brief peaks. Use them alongside the server's allocation logs, not as an exact per-request peak measurement.

Compare median first-text delay, decoding rate, total time, and the observed range. Also inspect output lengths and stop_type: an answer that hit the output limit may be incomplete. Five repetitions are an initial check, not enough evidence for a dependable p95 latency claim.

Keep answer quality in the experiment

For the Cedar fixture, check that the answer preserves Mira, the date, and duplicate IDs. It should also distinguish an unapproved budget from a known budget amount. A faster configuration that invents an amount fails this task.

Build a small fixed test set from the work you intend to do. Include a question answered by a detail near the end of a document, an extraction task with a required format, and a question whose answer is absent. Save the generated text before changing cache precision or switching to a smaller model.

A useful score is the number of tasks that meet your written acceptance rules. Keep those rules unchanged while comparing settings. Temperature zero reduces sampling variation, but numerical differences across backends and builds can still affect output.

Reduce the prompt before expanding the hardware budget

Once the runtime is measured, inspect what the application sends it. A chat assistant can accumulate old turns, repeated instructions, and irrelevant document chunks until most of its context carries little useful evidence.

For a document assistant with a 4,096-token context, this is one possible allocation:

These are application design choices, not model limits or measured token counts. Count the fully formatted prompt with the model's tokenizer. The input and reserved output must fit together.

Remove duplicate excerpts and retain passages that support the answer, including qualifications and conflicting evidence. Evaluate retrieval changes against the fixed question set. A shorter prompt is only useful when it still contains what the model needs. Once a configuration meets your latency target and quality checks, save its launch command, engine revision, model hashes, prompts, raw responses, and GPU logs together. That gives you a working profile you can revisit when a model update or a new workload changes the results.

items.title: AI Agent Memory (Part 1): Why Remembering Isn't the Same as Learning
items.author: ShaoTung Lien (練紹彤)
items.content:
AI agents preserve experience in histories, notes, and reusable instructions, then bring it back through search and retrieval. Their models also carry broad knowledge learned during training. But for memory to improve future behavior, it must help a system notice what matters, recognize a situation, and choose an appropriate action.

Memento: a life held together by notes

In Christopher Nolan's , Leonard struggles to form new lasting memories. He uses photographs, notes, and tattoos to work out what happened and what to do next.

The notes help him carry on. But which note does he find? What did it leave out? Does he read it correctly? He can keep a conclusion and lose the reason he trusted it.

That is a useful way to think about agent memory. A deployed language model usually does not change its after each conversation. These are the numerical settings it learned during training. Software around the model saves the history and brings information back when work resumes.

The comparison has limits. The model already knows a lot. It can reason about new information and help check its records. Still, the film gives us a good question: how does yesterday's note help with today's decision?

Four different things we mean by memory

Think about learning to cook.

helps you keep track of the pan and what to do next.

lets you recall the dinner you burned and what happened that evening.

is general knowledge, such as knowing that thin slices cook quickly.

helps you do things you have practiced, like moving the pan and adjusting the heat without talking yourself through every step.

These functions work together. They are not identical boxes, and a memory does not have to pass through them in order.

An agent's log can help it use a past event. Written instructions can help it carry out a task. But the files alone do not show that it remembers or acts the way a person does.

Knowledge in the model, continuity around it

During training, a model learns language, facts, relationships, and ways to solve problems. That knowledge is spread across its parameters. It is not a library of pages the model searches.

When we use it, we supply context: instructions, conversation, information found through search, and tool results. Examples and corrections in the context can change its answer without changing its parameters.

The is the software around the model. It manages tools, keeps track of the task, and decides what the model receives next. It can save chats, pull out lessons, find documents, or load a : reusable instructions, sometimes with scripts and supporting files.

This helps. A saved preference can improve tomorrow's answer. A tested script can make a task more reliable. But once a correction leaves context, something has to save it and bring it back when needed.

Experience changes what stands out

An experienced cook hears the sizzling change and lowers the heat. A beginner may hear the same sound and miss the warning. Practice helped the cook notice something useful.

We will use a few terms for this throughout the series:

  • what you want to achieve.
  • what you notice and focus on.
  • what you think you are looking at.
  • what you think is true or will happen next.
  • what you decide to believe or do.

These affect each other. If you expect trouble, you look more closely. If you see something surprising, you may change your expectation.

Human experiments show that past experience can guide attention even when we are not trying to recall it. People still forget and make bad calls. The useful point is that experience can change how we read the next situation.

Where the past can lose its influence

An agent saves a log, writes a lesson, and stores it. Later, search or a chooses what to bring into context. Some guidance is added automatically.

There are several ways this can go wrong. The lesson leaves out an exception. Its description does not match the new task. Or the agent finds the right note, but the situation has changed.

This is where I would look: did yesterday's experience help the agent notice the right thing and make a better choice today?

Memory is what we keep from the past. Learning is how the past changes what we do next.

Useful learning should help later work. Does the agent spot a familiar risk, change an outdated expectation, or choose a method with fewer reminders?

A saved rule, a better selector, or model training could help. External memory also gives us something we can read and correct.

More records alone do not prove . I want to see the agent still do the job well when the situation changes, including when an old method should not be used.

The next question is how the system knows which saved lesson matters now.

items.title: We Built a Test to Catch Contact Forms That Lie. It Lied to Us Five Times First
items.author: Formgong
items.content:
My team builds a form backend, and the most common message we get is some version of "my form stopped working". Usually the form never worked. Someone generated the site, clicked Send once, saw a green "Message sent!" and moved on. In early October we got tired of guessing how often that happens and decided to count it on sites built with Lovable and Bolt.

On paper the plan was short. Open a live site, find the contact form, fill it in with test values nobody would type for real, press Send and watch what leaves the page. If a request goes out with our text in it, the form sends. If nothing goes out and the page still celebrates, the form is fake. Every request after the click was blocked in the browser, so no site owner got a test message from us.

We wrote the rules down before the first site was tested. The test went through 793 sites and found 119 contact forms. It took six runs to get to the final answer, which was 27 fakes out of the 105 forms with a clear result.

Six runs, because the test itself kept getting things wrong. These are the five times it fooled us, more or less in the order we noticed.

1. Analytics looked like sending

Version one counted any request after the click as "the form sent something". If you've ever opened the network tab on a modern landing page, you can guess what happened. Pressing Send also pings Google Analytics, Tag Manager, Clarity, Hotjar, PostHog or Vercel's insights, and Lovable sites call their own analytics endpoint too. A fake form with three trackers on the page passed as a working one.

So "sends" got a stricter meaning. A request only counts if it carries what we typed. We picked test values that stand out, an address and a phone number starting with 555, which made them easy to find in a URL or a request body. Known analytics hosts were ignored on top of that.

2. The answer was in an alert box

During the pilot, one site cleared its fields after Send and that was it. No toast, no text, no request. It looked like a form that simply does nothing. It turned out the site had shown an , and the browser automation had dismissed it before we could read it.

After that, whatever a dialog said was treated as part of the page.

After the full run, we went through the fakes by hand. For each one we opened the site's JavaScript and read the submit handler. Most were exactly what we expected, and the pattern became familiar quickly: wait a second, show a green toast, reset the fields. No , no email service, no database.

But two forms we had confirmed as fake by reading their code were classed as "nothing happened". They showed "Message sent!" for two or three seconds and then hid it. Our test read the page once, five seconds after the click, by which point the toast was gone.

The fix was to sample the page every 250 milliseconds for five seconds and keep every new line of text we saw. In the same pass we found a form that sent people to by setting . Navigations like that never show up as network requests, so we hooked them separately.

4. Our test was the bot the honeypot was waiting for

This one is my favourite. A site returned a "queued" message, but its code clearly sent requests. On a closer look, the handler had a honeypot, a hidden field that only bots fill in. If the field has a value, the form quietly shows a fake success and drops the message. Our test filled every text field it could find, including that hidden one, so the site correctly treated us as a bot.

So the test stopped filling fields that a person can't see or reach. That created the next problem.

5. The wrong guess, then the real cause

After that change, three sites that had been sending started refusing our test values. We logged a diagnosis: the honeypot rule must be skipping ordinary fields named or . We narrowed the rule. Nothing changed.

The real cause took measuring rather than guessing. Those sites used shadcn/Radix select menus. A Radix select renders a hidden native , one pixel by one pixel, marked , and the form validates against it. Our "never fill hidden fields" rule now skipped it, the required select stayed empty, and the form refused to submit. Honeypots are text boxes, so the final rule only skips hidden text fields, and hidden selects and checkboxes get filled.

We're including the wrong guess on purpose. It went into the log as a diagnosis, and it was only a guess.

What we checked so we could trust the result

Every time the test changed, it had to pass a set of local pages where we knew the right answer: a fake toast, a real to an API, a native POST, a form, an analytics-only page, an AI chat box that isn't a contact form, and so on. By the end there were 23 of them, and the test classified all 23 correctly. We also ran a deliberately broken version of the classifier against the same pages. It got 10 of 23 right, which told us the pages could catch a broken test.

Of the 27 forms the final run called fake, we confirmed 21 by reading their submit handler. For the other 6 we couldn't find the handler in the minified bundle, so we report them as flagged by the test, not as proven.

Of the 105 forms with a clear result, 54 sent the message. 27 showed a success message and sent nothing. 12 did nothing a visitor could see. 7 opened the visitor's email app, 3 moved to another page without the message, and 2 just reloaded the page.

The obvious objection is that these are demos. We had the same thought, so before counting we sorted the sites by fixed rules. Demos, with hackathon entries and placeholder phone numbers, faked their forms in 9 of 15 cases. Among the 73 sites with no signs of being a demo, 16 faked it, and so did 5 of the 30 on their own domains.

The sample has limits. It came from public listings, which lean towards developer projects. Since we blocked every request, the test shows whether a form tried to send, not whether an email arrived. And it's one moment in time.

The AI tools build what a working form looks like from the outside, and a fake one looks exactly the same. You only see the difference in the network tab, or when a customer tells you they never heard back.

If you have a site with a form, open it in Chrome, press F12, go to Network, and send yourself a message. A new request with your text in it means the form works. Nothing new means it only says it does.

Have you ever written a test that turned out to be the bug? I'd like to hear your version in the comments.
