items.title: Can AI Write CAD? Testing LLM-Generated 3D Models for Manufacturability
items.author: Melody Cole
items.content:
1. Why I wanted to test this

I am a mechanical engineering student, and like most students I now see AI tools everywhere. They explain thermodynamics, debug my Python, and summarize papers. So one question kept bothering me: if an AI can write code, can it also write a ?

Code and CAD feel closely related. Tools like CadQuery and OpenSCAD let you describe a 3D part as a script, so in theory an LLM that writes the script can “design” a part from a text description.

But there is a gap between and . A script can execute without errors and still produce a bracket with 0.3 mm walls, holes that overlap the edge, or a gear that cannot mesh with anything. In engineering, “it ran” is not the same as “it is correct.” This article is my attempt, as a student, to define how to measure that gap honestly.

This is Part 1: the method. I am publishing the plan, the rules, and a verified reference script before the results, so that nobody (including me) can bend the criteria to fit the numbers.

2. Background: how CAD represents shapes

To judge AI-generated CAD, it helps to know what CAD software actually stores. Three ideas matter here.

Boundary representation (B-rep). Most mechanical CAD systems describe a solid by its boundary: faces, edges, and vertices, plus the topology that says how they connect. This is why you can select a face and add a fillet. A classic reference for how solids are represented and built up with operations such as union, cut, and intersect is Martti Mäntylä, An Introduction to Solid Modeling (Computer Science Press, 1988).

Constructive solid geometry (CSG). Here a shape is built as a tree of Boolean operations on primitives such as boxes, cylinders, and spheres. OpenSCAD follows this style (OpenSCAD documentation. It is intuitive and very scriptable, but it is mostly used to produce meshes such as STL files, which do not carry the exact faces and edges that B-rep CAD systems use for downstream engineering work.

NURBS and freeform surfaces.

Curved surfaces in CAD are commonly described with NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines). The standard reference is Les Piegl and Wayne Tiller, , 2nd ed. (Springer, 1997). My understanding is that this is part of why operations like fillets and shells can fail on complex geometry: the kernel has to build new surfaces that stay valid and watertight.

For a broader view of the mathematics behind curves, surfaces, and solids, Michael E. Mortenson, , 3rd ed. (Industrial Press, 2006) describes and compares the important methods.

Parametric modeling and design intent

The word matters a lot in this test. A parametric model is driven by named values (length, thickness, hole diameter), so changing one value updates the whole part correctly. The real skill in CAD is not drawing shapes. It is capturing : which dimensions are free, which are constrained, and what must stay true when something changes. A model with hard-coded numbers scattered through the code looks like CAD but behaves like a dead drawing. I treat this as a key test.

3. Code-based CAD: CadQuery and a reference script

I am using , a Python module for building parametric 3D CAD models that is based on the OpenCASCADE kernel and can export STEP files; shape objects expose checks such as and (CadQuery documentation, I chose code-based CAD for one practical reason: it makes the test reproducible and checkable. I can run the same script on any machine, measure the result with code, and keep everything in version control.

Below is the reference part, an L-bracket with four mounting holes. It shows what “design intent in code” looks like: every dimension is a named parameter, the hole layout is derived from those parameters, and asserts stop the script if the parameters conflict.

import math
import cadquery as cq

# ---- Parameters (all in millimetres) ----
length       = 80.0   # base length along X
width        = 40.0   # bracket width along Y
thickness    = 4.0    # base and wall thickness
height       = 50.0   # overall height along Z
hole_dia     = 6.5    # clearance hole for an M6 bolt
hole_inset   = 10.0   # hole centre to the free end and to each side edge
hole_pitch_x = 30.0   # spacing between the two hole columns along X

# ---- Hole layout, derived from the parameters ----
x_far  = length - hole_inset        # column nearest the free end
x_near = x_far - hole_pitch_x       # second column, toward the wall
y_edge = width / 2 - hole_inset     # two rows at +/- y_edge
hole_pts = [(x_near, -y_edge), (x_near, y_edge),
            (x_far,  -y_edge), (x_far,  y_edge)]

# ---- Design-intent checks: fail early if parameters conflict ----
r = hole_dia / 2
assert x_near - r > thickness, "holes would hit the vertical wall"
assert y_edge + r < width / 2, "holes would break through the side edge"
assert x_far + r < length,     "holes would break through the free end"

# ---- L-shaped profile in the XZ plane, extruded symmetrically across Y ----
bracket = (
    cq.Workplane("XZ")
    .polyline([
        (0, 0), (length, 0), (length, thickness),
        (thickness, thickness), (thickness, height), (0, height),
    ])
    .close()
    .extrude(width / 2, both=True)
)

# ---- Cut the mounting holes through the base ----
cutter = (
    cq.Workplane("XY")
    .workplane(offset=-1)
    .pushPoints(hole_pts)
    .circle(r)
    .extrude(thickness + 2)
)
bracket = bracket.cut(cutter)

# ---- Validity checks against a hand calculation ----
solid = bracket.val()
profile_area = length * thickness + (height - thickness) * thickness
expected_volume = profile_area * width - len(hole_pts) * math.pi * r**2 * thickness
bb = solid.BoundingBox()

print("Valid solid:", solid.isValid())
print("Solids:", len(bracket.solids().vals()))
print("Volume (mm^3):", round(solid.Volume(), 1), "expected:", round(expected_volume, 1))
print("Bounding box (mm):", round(bb.xlen, 1), round(bb.ylen, 1), round(bb.zlen, 1))
assert solid.isValid()
assert abs(solid.Volume() - expected_volume) < 1.0

cq.exporters.export(bracket, "bracket.step")
cq.exporters.export(bracket, "bracket.stl")

The hand calculation is what makes the checks meaningful. The L-profile area is 80 × 4 + 46 × 4 = 504 mm², and extruding it across the 40 mm width gives 20,160 mm³. The four holes (6.5 mm diameter, 4 mm deep) remove about 531 mm³. So when the script runs correctly it should report a volume of about and a bounding box of 80 × 40 × 50 mm. If a generated script disagrees with these numbers, something is wrong even if it runs. Change from 4 to 6 and the profile, the holes, and the checks all still hold.

I picked parts in increasing order of difficulty, to see where the models start to break:

L-bracket with 4 mounting holes

Basic extrusion, hole placement, units

Flanged shaft coupling with keyway

Revolved geometry, standard-style features, tolerances

Spur gear (specified module, teeth, bore)

Mathematical geometry (involute profile), constraints

Electronics enclosure with lid and snap-fit

Multiple bodies, wall thickness, fits and clearances

Bolt, nut, and plate assembly

Assembly relationships, thread representation, clearances

Each part comes with a written specification: dimensions, units, material, and intended manufacturing process (FDM 3D printing for parts 1, 4, and 5; CNC machining for parts 2 and 3).

Every model receives the for each part, built from four pieces: the part description with all dimensions in millimetres; the target library (CadQuery) and its version; a request to put all dimensions in a parameter block at the top; and a request to include basic validity checks.

I test two conditions. In the first, the model gets one attempt. In the second, I give the model the error message or a plain description of the failed check and allow up to three repair prompts. This mirrors how people actually use these tools.

For every run I record the exact model name and version, the test date, the Python and CadQuery versions, the operating system, and any printer, slicer, and material used. All prompts and raw outputs are saved unedited in a repository.

Pass/fail criteria (fixed before testing)

I define these rules before looking at any output, so I cannot bend them to fit the results. The thresholds are my own choices for this small test.

  • the script runs to the end with no exception in the recorded CadQuery version, with no manual edits.
  • exactly one solid, is true, and the volume is positive.
  • overall dimensions within 0.5 mm of the specification, and hole diameters and positions within 0.1 mm.
  • after I change each key parameter by 25 percent, the script still builds one valid solid and every dependent feature follows.
  • Manufacturable (digital): passes every applicable rule in Section 5 for the stated process.
  • STEP and STL files are written and open in a viewer (and in a slicer for printed parts).

Levels of human intervention

  1. the model’s original output, run unedited.
  2. after up to three follow-up prompts that contain only the error message or a plain description of the failed check.
  3. I edited the code myself. I count the lines changed and report these separately, never as a model success.

I score each output from 0 to 5 on five criteria, where 0 means it fails completely, 3 means it is usable after manual edits, and 5 means it passes with no edits.

Does the script run without errors?

Do the dimensions and features match the specification?

Does changing a parameter update the model correctly?

Would it print or machine without redesign?

Would a reviewer accept the design decisions (fits, wall thickness, load paths)?

5. What “manufacturable” means here

A valid CAD model or a clean STEP export does not prove that a part can be made. In this article, a digital manufacturability evaluation means I check the geometry against the process rules below. A means a part is actually printed or machined. Unless I say a part was physically made, every manufacturability result is digital.

I use two layers of checks. First, automated checks in code: is it one valid solid, is the volume positive and close to a hand calculation, do the bounding box dimensions match the specification, and does it export cleanly to STEP and STL?

Second, an engineering review of the kind taught in a design class.

For design for manufacturing (DFM) thinking, I lean on Geoffrey Boothroyd, Peter Dewhurst, and Winston A. Knight, Product Design for Manufacture and Assembly, 3rd ed. (CRC Press, 2011), and on Karl T. Ulrich, Steven D. Eppinger, and Maria C. Yang, Product Design and Development, 7th ed.

(McGraw-Hill Education, 2020), which has a chapter on design for manufacturing and supply chain. For additive manufacturing constraints I use Ian Gibson, David Rosen, and Brent Stucker, Additive Manufacturing Technologies: 3D Printing, Rapid Prototyping, and Direct Digital Manufacturing, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2015), which includes a chapter on design for additive manufacturing.

For dimensions and fits, I check tolerances against David A. Madsen, David P. Madsen, and Dennis A. Schwartz, Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing: Principles and Practices, 10th ed. (Goodheart-Willcox, 2021), which follows the ASME Y14.5-2018 standard. For basic design calculations such as bolt sizing, I use Richard G. Budynas and J. Keith Nisbett, Shigley’s Mechanical Engineering Design, 11th ed.

(McGraw-Hill Education, 2020), which includes a chapter on screws, fasteners, and nonpermanent joints.

The rules below are common rules of thumb, so always confirm the limits for your own printer, material, and machine shop.

  • Wall thickness at least a small multiple of the nozzle diameter
  • Overhangs steeper than roughly 45 degrees need support or redesign
  • Printed holes tend to come out slightly undersized, so clearance fits need allowance
  • Moving or mating parts need deliberate clearance gaps
  • Internal corners need a radius because cutting tools are round
  • Very deep, narrow holes are hard to drill and clear chips from
  • Features must be reachable by a tool from some direction

6. Failure modes I will be looking for

These are known risks in code generation and CAD scripting, not findings from my tests. In Part 2, I will report only failures I actually observed, and for each one I will say what the model did, how I detected it, and whether the repair worked.

1. Invented or unsupported function calls. Code-generating models can produce code that reads well but fails when run. Mark Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code (arXiv:2107.03374, 2021), judged code models by functional correctness (does the program actually work?) rather than by text similarity, and reported limits such as difficulty with long chains of operations and with binding operations to variables. Calling CadQuery methods that do not exist is one form this can take in my setting.

2. Coordinate and workplane confusion. CAD scripting depends on knowing which plane you are sketching on and which way is “up.” A feature can end up on the wrong side of a part or at the wrong height.

3. Unit and dimension drift. A model may switch between millimetres and inches, or misread a diameter as a radius.

A script can look parametric because it has a parameter block, yet use raw numbers in the geometry code, which breaks design intent as soon as a value changes.

5. Operations that fail on real geometry. Fillets, chamfers, and shells can fail when the model picks the wrong edges or the geometry makes the operation invalid. This relates to the boundary-representation operations described in Section 2.

6. Looks right, but not manufacturable. A part can match the specification on paper and still have thin walls, unsupported overhangs, or no clearance for assembly.

A spur gear needs a correct tooth profile, and small errors mean gears that will not mesh.

I will evaluate each generated CAD model using the same criteria to keep the comparison consistent. The evaluation will cover five test parts: an L-bracket, a shaft coupling, a spur gear, an electronics enclosure, and a bolt-nut-plate assembly.

For each part, I will check:

  • Does the generated script run without errors?
  • Do the dimensions and features match the specification?
  • Does the model produce the expected valid geometry?
  • Does the model update correctly when key dimensions change?
  • Digital manufacturability: Does the geometry meet the predefined requirements for its intended manufacturing process?
  • Can the model be exported and opened in the required formats?
  • How many repair prompts or manual code changes are needed?

I will evaluate the original output separately from the output produced after up to three repair prompts. Any manual corrections will be documented separately and will not count as an unmodified AI success.

No scores or comparative results are reported here because the experiments have not yet been completed. Part 2 will present the observations, measurements, and supporting evidence collected during the tests.

8. Limitations of this test

  • Five parts and a handful of models is not a statistically strong study.
  • One library and one workflow. Results may differ with other CAD scripting tools or prompting styles.
  • AI models change quickly, so any results will describe only the versions and dates I record.
  • Parts of the “engineering sense” score involve subjective review, even with a rubric.
  • Unless I state that a part was printed or machined, manufacturability is judged on the geometry and the rules above.
  • No claim about all AI models. Results will describe only the models, library versions, and parts I test.

So, My hypothesis, as a student who spends a lot of time checking dimensions, is that it can write CAD , and sometimes that code will produce a usable part, but “usable” will still depend on a human who understands the geometry, the manufacturing process, and the design intent. The test above is how I plan to find out whether that is true or just a comfortable guess.

What I believe so far is that the hard part of CAD was never typing. It is knowing what the part needs to do, how it will be made, and what could go wrong. If AI speeds up the first draft, the fundamentals taught in design, manufacturing, and tolerancing courses matter more, not less.

items.title: Media Titan Omri Hurwitz: Humans, Not Bots, Run the News
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
When first appeared on as one of its earliest guests, he made a remark about AI and the news that James Spiro later used as a headline. Returning for , the CEO of was asked what had changed. His answer was steady: “AI still does not write the news.” Most media outlets, he said, maintain a strong editorial policy in which AI may help draft a post, develop ideas, fine-tune the writing, or suggest headlines, while a good, strong human editor makes the final call on what gets published.

What happened to AI-run outlets

Hurwitz described several recent experiments in which AI agents were set up to run an entire media outlet, acting as writer, editor, and decision-maker on what to cover. He chose not to name the projects, but he said none lasted more than three or four months. The outlets did not gather enough readers, he said, their distribution was limited, and their story selection did not match what people wanted to read. Whatever the technical thesis behind each experiment, the audience verdict was the one that counted.

His conclusion was about the reader rather than the technology. “People want to consume content from real people,” Hurwitz said. Spiro agreed with the principle and added a refinement from his own routine: audiences want content from real people, but AI can serve as the aggregator that surfaces it. Hurwitz did not dispute the refinement, and the exchange set up the show’s broader discussion of how AI and human editors can each do what they do best.

AI as a personal aggregator

Spiro described the setup he uses. An automation running on his language models sends a tailored briefing to his phone every afternoon, working in effect as a personal newsletter that opens with “Here are some of the top stories that you may have missed.” Each item comes with an explanation of why it matters for his sector, for the country where he lives, and for the stories he is writing. The stories themselves, he said, are hopefully written by humans, and “AI has kind of personalized it for me.”

That use case captures the balance both men described. The reporting and the editorial judgment stay with people, and AI helps readers find what is relevant to them in a crowded news flow. Hurwitz’s own firm applies a similar sensibility to distribution. Omri Hurwitz Media runs a PR practice for more than 60 companies, about 16 of them unicorns, among them Upwind Security, and a media acquisition practice with more than $16 million in direct equity in U.S. outlets. Part of what the firm brings to those outlets is stronger social distribution, including paid ads and Twitter arbitrage.

Hurwitz was optimistic when the discussion moved to how AI systems source information. He noted that the shaping of information is not new. Before language models, he said, the organizations that invested most in search optimization could influence what people saw on Google, and before the internet, gatekeepers such as major newspapers set the terms. “It has always been like that,” Hurwitz said, and he thinks today’s audiences have more choice than any before them. He called it a great time to decide what information to take in, and he was confident that “AI will not interfere with that.”

Spiro noted that the field is still young. He recalled a reflection that people operate in a kind of fog and only see the road they took when they look back, and he suggested that people may someday ask why every platform did not adopt community notes sooner. He welcomed experiments such as the one by Steven Bartlett, whose podcast embeds community notes in the show before it airs and surfaces them as pop-ups on YouTube. For Spiro, accountability delivered in real time and from the grassroots is a promising direction.

The conversation also touched on AI companies becoming media owners. For OpenAI, the entry point was TBPN, the daily tech show it acquired in April and which now reports into its chief global affairs officer. In Europe, ETN, a daily show in the same style, gathered a $1.6 million seed round and expanded to five days a week, with Axel Springer, OpenAI, and DeepMind among its investors. On the platform side, Spotify’s reported $200 million licensing deal for The Joe Rogan Experience was renewed in 2024 and 2026, estimated at $250 million each time. Hurwitz disclosed that his company is trying to buy equity in ETN.

Hurwitz suggested separating two questions. One is media acquisition, which he sees as part of a long history of owners and audiences finding each other. The other is how language models weigh and balance their sources, which he called a matter for their engineers. His overall explanation for the investment wave was short: “it’s eyeballs, brand capital, institutional capital.” His example was Alex Cooper’s podcast: once it is bigger than a CNN segment, brands follow, and institutions after them.

What this means for builders of audiences

For writers and hosts, the lesson Hurwitz drew is that the personal voice remains the asset, with AI as a helper. He said creators can earn from brands, from institutions, and directly from subscribers, and Spiro added that a niche audience of the right people can be enough. Spiro is growing The Spiro Circle for techies interested in Israel, cyber, and geopolitics, and he said its value will rest on disclosure, independence, and a willingness to correct mistakes. In an age of automated writing, the people behind a publication are what readers come back for.

items.title: Turning Product Info into Video Ads: Our Experience with Vizard Agent
items.author: Alex Bennett
items.content:
Nowadays, having enough product material is rarely the main problem for e-commerce operators. Amazon listings may already contain product images, descriptions, key features, pricing information, and other commercial assets. The harder part is turning those materials into enough video creatives for advertising campaigns without spending hours on scripting, editing, and producing variations.

Therefore, we tested Vizard Agent from this perspective, focusing on a common scenario in which an e-commerce operator has plenty of product information but needs to produce a large number of promotional videos. The test looked particularly at its Amazon Product Link to Promo Video workflow, as well as its UGC-style and advertising function.

The starting point was quiet simple. Instead of preparing a complete video production package, the workflow begins with an Amazon product listing URL. Vizard's Ads mode allows sellers to paste an Amazon listing URL and have Vizard Agent extract product visuals and product details as the basis for video creation. The workflow can also start from uploaded product images, descriptions, and key features when a URL is not the preferred input.

This approach fits the broader design of Vizard Agent. The Agent can work with links, existing footage, files, or combinations of user materials and generated assets. It interprets the request, plans the video, selects or creates assets, makes creative decisions, assembles the result, and reviews the finished video. For an e-commerce operator, that changes the starting point considerably. The product listing itself can become the creative brief rather than simply a reference that someone has to manually read before beginning production.

The workflow is useful because it connects product information with the actual video production process. After providing the listing, the user can specify the desired video type by giving the prompts, such as a product showcase, lifestyle-oriented video, or promotional advertisement. Vizard Agent then adapts the visual treatment to the requested format. Product images and descriptions provide the foundation, while subtitles, voiceover, visual elements, and other creative components can be incorporated into the finished video. This is where the workflow becomes more practical than simply converting an image into a slideshow. The purpose is to turn product information into a structured promotional story. Instead of deciding manually which product feature should appear first, writing the script, selecting supporting visuals, and arranging the scenes one by one, the operator can give the Agent the product and the intended advertising goal.

Vizard's documented product-ad workflow also covers product pages to video ads, product images to UGC-style ads, multiple advertising angles for one product, variations from a winning advertisement, and seasonal campaign variations.

For high-volume e-commerce campaigns, the ability to move from one product to several creative directions is arguably more important than producing one polished video.

The UGC mode was one of the more practical parts of the test. We started with the same product materials rather than preparing a separate batch of creator footage, and used the product images as the basis for a UGC-style ad. The result was noticeably different from a conventional product showcase, with the product positioned within a more creator-oriented advertising format.

What worked particularly well here was the amount of preparation Vizard Agent handled on its own. We did not have to build a separate UGC script, work out the structure manually, or assemble the product visuals scene by scene. Vizard Agent allows product images to be turned into UGC-style ads and treats the creative process as a broader video-production task rather than a sequence of individual editing operations.From a testing perspective, the more interesting point was that the same product assets could be taken in different directions without restarting the production process. We could use the product information for a conventional promotional video, then move toward a UGC-style treatment when a different advertising angle was needed. For an e-commerce operator producing creatives at scale, that flexibility was more valuable than simply having another editing option.

Why This Matters for High-Volume Advertising

The biggest advantage we observed was not a single editing feature. It was the reduction in the number of production decisions required from the operator. A conventional workflow might require a marketer to read the listing, identify selling points, write a hook, develop a script, gather product visuals, edit the footage, add captions and voiceover, and then repeat much of the process for another advertising concept.

Vizard Agent approaches these activities as one broader production task. Its documented workflow covers understanding the request, planning the video, selecting or creating assets, making creative and editing decisions, assembling the video, and reviewing the result. That becomes particularly valuable when one product needs ten creative variations rather than one finished advertisement. The platform's documented support for multiple ad angles, variations from winning ads, and seasonal versions directly addresses this type of production volume.

Vizard Agent is most relevant to Amazon sellers, DTC brands, e-commerce marketers, agencies, and performance marketing teams that already have substantial product information but need to increase their video output. It is also useful when the same product needs to appear in different creative formats across short-form channels. Vizard's Amazon product video workflow is not limited to Amazon itself. Generated videos can also be used across social and advertising channels such as Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts.

What Still Requires Human Review

We should declare that AI’s work does not remove the need for human oversight. Product claims, pricing, brand requirements, campaign objectives, and platform policies still need to be checked before publication. The quality of the source listing also matters because the Agent is working from the information and assets available to it. That limitation is important for Amazon sellers in particular. Automating production does not automatically make an advertisement accurate or commercially appropriate. Human review remains necessary, especially when a video makes specific product claims.

For the e-commerce scenario we tested, Vizard Agent is more useful to think of as a video production agent than as another AI editing tool. The Amazon Product Link to Promo Video workflow provides a particularly straightforward entry point. An existing product listing can become the starting material for a promotional video, while UGC-style creation and multiple advertising angles allow the same product information to support different creative approaches. For e-commerce teams that already have plenty of product material but struggle with the volume of video they need to produce, that workflow reduction is the main value. The interesting shift is not simply that AI can edit a video faster. It is that the product listing, creative brief, asset selection, scripting, editing, and variation process can increasingly be treated as one production task.

items.title: When AI Works Perfectly, What Happens to Human Life?
items.author: Kosuke Shirako
items.content:
The medical report says there is nothing wrong. Every number falls within its expected range. No abnormality has been detected. The system has done what it was designed to do.

And yet, on the morning before work, the body hesitates. It knows something that the report cannot describe. Or perhaps it knows nothing at all. Perhaps the sensation is ordinary anxiety, fatigue, or a passing discomfort. The distinction matters, but the person experiencing it cannot yet make that distinction.

The report is correct. The discomfort remains. There is no contradiction in the data. Only a contradiction in the life that must continue after the data has been delivered.

This is where a story might begin. Not with a malfunctioning machine, but with a functioning one.

The World in Which Nothing Goes Wrong

Much of our imagination about artificial intelligence remains organized around failure. We fear the incorrect diagnosis, the discriminatory algorithm, the autonomous system that escapes its instructions. We imagine machines that deceive, disobey, or misunderstand us. These dangers are real enough to deserve serious attention.

But another kind of future is harder to picture. A future in which the systems become remarkably good. They identify illness earlier. They match workers with appropriate jobs. They calculate risks, recommend careers, preserve memories, and relieve us of countless small decisions. The machinery of everyday life becomes smoother. There are fewer mistakes to correct, fewer uncertainties to endure, fewer reasons to question the next recommendation.

And yet, somewhere inside this increasingly orderly world, a person stops. Not because the system has failed. Because the system's success has revealed something it was never built to understand. What happens when the answer is correct, but the question was incomplete?

This question became the starting point for LIFE, a ten-part work of linked fiction developed by SHIRO & Co., an independent creative and research practice in Tokyo. LIFE is not a story about artificial intelligence taking over the world. It is about the quieter possibility that the world might remain recognizable even as something essential becomes difficult to name.

Engineers have good reasons to dislike friction. Friction slows processes, introduces uncertainty, increases costs, and creates opportunities for failure. To remove it is often to improve a system.

But in human life, friction has another meaning. It is the pause before saying something irreversible. It is the embarrassment of being inexperienced, the uncertainty of beginning a relationship, the inability to explain why a familiar place suddenly feels different. It is the interval between knowing what is reasonable and deciding what one can live with.

Not all of these experiences are valuable. Some are painful, unnecessary, even destructive. But neither are they all defects awaiting correction.

Consider a young person applying for a first job. The recruitment system asks for experience. It evaluates qualifications accurately, compares candidates fairly according to its criteria, and produces a defensible decision. The applicant has no experience. The answer is no. Nothing in the system needs to be broken for the rejection to make sense. Yet a question remains: where does experience begin, in a society that increasingly requires it before granting entry?

The problem is not simply that a machine has evaluated a person. It is that the criteria of evaluation may quietly determine which kinds of lives are allowed to begin. We can improve the algorithm. We can revise its criteria. We can introduce exceptions. But sooner or later we encounter a question that is not exclusively computational. Who is willing to make room for someone who has not yet become useful?

A Future That Has Not Happened

In another story, a thirteen-year-old faces a future already arranged according to stability and probability. The recommendations are sensible. Certain paths offer better prospects. Others carry greater risks. The system has no reason to conceal what it knows. Parents might find such guidance reassuring.

But there is an awkward fact about childhood: the person whose future is being predicted does not yet fully exist. Not in the sense that the child is incomplete or lacks a voice. Rather, the future person will be shaped by encounters, disappointments, friendships, accidents, and desires that have not yet occurred. A recommendation can describe likely outcomes. It cannot contain every possibility that will emerge from living.

There is a profound difference between helping someone imagine a future and deciding, in advance, which future is worth imagining. This distinction is easy to lose when prediction becomes increasingly persuasive. The more accurate a recommendation appears, the more difficult it can become to disagree with it. Eventually, refusing the optimal choice may begin to look like an error.

Yet the freedom to become someone unexpected has always depended, at least partly, on the right to make choices whose value cannot be demonstrated beforehand.

The Things a System Can Remember

Memory presents another difficulty. Imagine an old message, left on an online bulletin board twenty years ago. The original conversation has ended. The participants have changed, disappeared, or perhaps died. The message remains.

Then a reply arrives. It resembles a continuation of the conversation, but the voice is not the voice of the person who originally wrote it.

Technically, information has been preserved and reproduced. Something has survived. But what exactly? A person's words are not the same as that person's continued presence. A voice is not a life. A convincing response does not restore the circumstances in which an earlier conversation took place.

Still, the response may move us. We may recognize something in it. We may even find comfort. It would be too simple to declare that such experiences are false, just as it would be too simple to treat them as equivalent to human continuity. Between those positions lies a region that ordinary technological language struggles to describe.

Literature has lived in that region for centuries. It knows that memory can be inaccurate and still meaningful. That absence can remain present. That a silence may carry more of a relationship than a complete transcript.

AI introduces new possibilities for preserving traces of human life. It does not settle what those traces mean.

LIFE exists as ten interconnected stories, accompanied by microdramas that approach its questions through brief audiovisual experiences.

At first glance, microdrama might seem an unlikely format for philosophical inquiry. There is little time for explanation. No space for an elaborate argument. Often, barely enough room for a situation to unfold.

But that limitation is precisely what makes the form interesting.

A person looks at a screen. A sentence appears. Someone hesitates before responding. The scene ends. The viewer has been given almost no explanation, yet something continues beyond the final image.

Unlike an explanatory video, a microdrama does not necessarily tell its audience what to think. It can place a contradiction before them and leave the work of interpretation unfinished. This is not a rejection of analysis. It is another way of beginning it.

For people who design AI systems, fiction offers an unusual perspective. Technical evaluations ask whether a system behaves correctly under specified conditions. Stories ask what happens to a person who must continue living after the system has behaved correctly. The distinction matters. A model may complete its task. A human experience does not necessarily end there.

What Cannot Be Captured by an Output

When software behaves according to its specification, we have a basis for calling it correct.

But human situations rarely arrive with complete specifications. A request may be clearly expressed while the underlying desire remains uncertain. A recommendation may be justified while the consequences are emotionally unbearable. A decision may satisfy every formal requirement and still leave someone unable to move forward.

This does not make correctness irrelevant. It makes correctness insufficient as a complete description of human experience.

As AI systems become more deeply involved in consequential decisions, a distinction becomes necessary between producing an answer and possessing the authority to act on it. An observation is not yet a recommendation. A recommendation is not yet a decision. And a decision is not always the end of the matter.

Sometimes the appropriate response is to ask another question. Sometimes it is to acknowledge that the available evidence cannot settle the issue. Sometimes it is to allow a person to refuse a reasonable recommendation without having to prove that the system was wrong.

This is not a romantic argument for irrationality. It is a recognition that human judgment involves more than selecting the best option from a defined set. It also involves deciding whether the available options adequately describe the situation. The ability to say not yet may be as important as the ability to say yes or no.

An Ending That Does Not Resolve

The ten stories of LIFE move through health, work, intimacy, education, aging, memory, and observation. Their settings change, but a similar tension returns. The systems work. The world continues. And something remains outside the record.

It might be a bodily sensation, an unchosen future, a voice that no longer belongs to its speaker, or a feeling for which no useful category exists.

None of these things proves that technology should retreat from human life. Nor does their existence mean that suffering, uncertainty, and inefficiency should be preserved for their own sake.

The question is more modest, and perhaps more difficult. Can we build increasingly capable systems without treating everything they cannot resolve as an imperfection? Can a system be useful without becoming authoritative? Can technology leave space for experiences that do not improve a metric, complete a workflow, or produce a satisfactory conclusion?

Literature offers no engineering specification for such a world. It has something else to offer: attention to what happens between the events we know how to measure.

A machine produces an answer. A person reads it. The screen goes quiet. Outside, the day continues. There are trains to catch, messages to answer, people to meet, things that cannot be postponed.

The answer may be correct. The person still has to live. And perhaps that is where the story begins.

LIFE is a ten-part literary anthology with accompanying microdrama experiences, developed by SHIRO & Co., an independent creative and research practice based in Tokyo. The project examines everyday life in a society where AI systems function as intended, yet human experiences continue to resist complete representation.

items.title: Sellvia in 2026: The Tech Behind Its Digital Stores, Built-In Ads, and Orders
items.author: Nica Furs
items.content:
Opening an ecommerce store used to involve several separate projects. A seller needed a website, hosting, product pages, payment tools, marketing software, and a system for keeping track of orders. None of those tasks was impossible, but the number of services involved made a small online business surprisingly complicated to operate.

Sellvia takes a more integrated approach. Instead of asking users to assemble a store from independent services, the platform provides a managed storefront, access to a product catalog, promotional tools, and a dashboard for everyday operations.

That approach is timely. Sellvia appeared at No. 591 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of fast-growing private companies in the United States. Beyond the ranking, the more interesting story is how the platform brings several parts of digital commerce into one workflow.

Sellvia is an ecommerce platform that helps users launch an online store and manage its day-to-day operations. Its turnkey store offering is based on WordPress with Sellvia's own plugin and managed hosting.

The company supplies a ready-to-use store structure rather than leaving the owner to configure a server and assemble a large collection of plugins. Product management, store activity, and available marketing tools are reached through the Sellvia Dashboard.

This design changes the work involved in getting started. A new owner can spend more time choosing products, improving descriptions, and planning how to reach customers. They spend less time on hosting arrangements and the technical maintenance of separate systems.

The platform is especially interesting for someone who wants to run a store without becoming a WordPress administrator. Sellvia manages much of the underlying environment, while users work with the controls provided in the dashboard.

The Product Catalog: A Faster Route to a Digital Store

One of Sellvia's practical advantages is access to an existing product catalog.

Digital products can include ebooks, downloadable guides, educational material, courses, and templates. Unlike physical merchandise, these products do not require a warehouse or parcel delivery. Customers receive access to digital content after completing the relevant purchase process.

Take a store specializing in productivity and professional development. The owner might organize useful digital resources around planning, career skills, or personal organization. The work becomes selecting coherent offers and presenting them clearly instead of sourcing physical inventory and arranging shipping.

Product quality and relevance still matter. A broad catalog is most useful when the store has a clear audience and a sensible way of helping visitors choose among available products.

This is also why digital commerce is an attractive starting point for an integrated platform: product presentation, customer purchase, and content delivery can be coordinated electronically.

The key to understanding Sellvia is to look beyond the storefront itself.

The is the public-facing part of the business. It presents products, organizes categories, and gives visitors a place to browse.

The supplies the items the owner can select and publish. This reduces the preparation involved in building a store from an empty website.

provides a managed promotional service within Sellvia's ecosystem. Users can review the available promotion settings and activity through their account rather than building the entire advertising workflow from scratch.

brings transaction records and order activity into the dashboard, helping users see which orders need attention and which have progressed through the applicable processing steps.

connects these activities. Instead of judging the business only by how the homepage looks, users can monitor product activity, promotion, and orders in one working environment.

These functions have different jobs, but they share a practical purpose: reducing the number of disconnected tools a store owner needs to manage.

Marketing is often the next challenge after a store goes live. Having a finished website does not mean that people will automatically discover its products.

Sellvia Ads addresses part of that challenge with a managed promotion service. Its published terms describe promotion through Sellvia-operated digital properties and internal placement systems. Available budgets and service options are managed from the platform environment.

That makes Sellvia Ads different from an ordinary advertising account in which a merchant manually controls every external placement. It is important to understand that the internal promotion service does not necessarily function as a campaign sending visitors directly to the owner's branded website.

For someone new to advertising, a managed service can reduce the number of settings they need to learn at the beginning. It also provides a convenient starting point for examining how promotional activity relates to product demand.

The useful metrics are the ones tied to business decisions: what promotion was used, which products generated activity, and how actual orders compare with promotional spending. Advertised exposure is not the same as a completed order, and keeping those measurements separate leads to better decisions.

From Product Listing to Digital Access

The digital-order journey is short enough to understand without technical jargon.

First, a product is selected from the catalog and presented to customers through the relevant store or sales interface. The product page should explain what the buyer receives and make the offer easy to evaluate.

Next, the customer completes the checkout process available for that purchase. The precise payment flow depends on the store's configured arrangement.

Once the purchase has been processed, the buyer can receive access to the digital material through the applicable delivery process. The order is also recorded in the systems used to manage store activity.

These steps show the practical value of selling downloadable resources: there is no shipping label, carrier pickup, or warehouse dispatch between a completed digital purchase and access to the purchased material.

The store owner should still test the experience personally. Product pages, checkout instructions, access links, and order records should be clear and consistent, particularly on mobile devices.

What Can a Store Owner Manage in the Dashboard?

A useful ecommerce dashboard should support decisions, not merely display numbers.

Sellvia groups important store functions in a central workspace. Users can work with the catalog, review order information, access available promotional controls, and inspect reporting provided for their account.

For example, an owner who has added several digital guides can check whether visitors are engaging with those offers and whether the products are generating orders. When experimenting with promotion, the same owner can compare activity over time and decide which subjects deserve more attention.

Centralization matters because small operational tasks accumulate. Every additional service normally introduces another login, another set of settings, and another place where data might need to be checked. A connected dashboard reduces that fragmentation.

For additional explanations of the interface and individual features, Sellvia.info provides platform-focused guides and resources.

Pricing and What Is Included

Sellvia's published September 2026 terms describe three base subscription levels:

The standard introductory offer described in those terms includes a 14-day trial. The availability of higher tiers and promotional offers may be subject to additional conditions.

The base subscription covers the relevant store infrastructure and platform access. Services such as advertising and certain order-related operations can have separate charges, so the subscription amount should not be mistaken for the total cost of operating a store.

A sensible first budget separates recurring software costs from optional promotion. That makes it much easier to test the platform methodically and understand the economics of a specific product category.

A Practical Way to Evaluate Sellvia

Before investing heavily in advertising, run through the service as both a store owner and a customer.

Review the catalog and select products that fit a recognizable audience. Check that each description makes the content and intended buyer clear. Open the storefront on a phone and make sure the navigation and product pages are readable.

Then inspect the purchase path that applies to your configuration, including what happens after checkout and how buyers obtain their digital content.

Finally, review the dashboard's order and promotion tools. Identify the information that will help you compare products and measure spending. These simple checks reveal much more about everyday usability than a feature list alone.

This kind of evaluation is also a useful way to understand the platform's central benefit: the work of running a digital store is organized around one connected operating environment.

Why the Integrated Approach Matters

Sellvia's model reflects a wider change in ecommerce software. Increasingly, the appeal of a platform is not just how quickly it creates a website but how much routine operational work it brings together afterward.

A hosted store, existing product catalog, built-in promotion, order management, and accessible reporting each solve a different problem. Their combined value is that owners spend less time coordinating software and more time understanding products and customers.

That does not replace sound business decisions. Choosing useful products, describing them accurately, managing expenses, and serving customers still matter.

But for someone who wants a practical way to begin selling digital products, Sellvia provides an integrated starting point. Its 2026 ecosystem shows how the storefront has become one component of a broader digital-commerce workspace.

items.title: LinearB Launches Agentic Studio to Steer AI Coding Agents in a $127 Billion Market by 2032
items.author: Ishan Pandey
items.content:
Developers who used AI on at least 75% of their coding days merged a median of 95.7% more pull requests per week in May 2026 than they did in June 2025 according to LinearB's benchmarks of 2.7 million pull requests from 253 engineering organizations, yet at the top-performing organizations in that same sample only 79% of the pull requests opened by autonomous agents merge within 30 days against 92% for changes written by humans alone.

LinearB, a Leader in the first Gartner Magic Quadrant for Developer Productivity Insight Platforms, launched Agentic Studio to close that gap by giving engineering leaders and coding agents the same view of everything that has happened across software delivery. The launch matters to anyone paying for AI coding tools because the benchmark data shows the extra code piling up in review queues and the token bill climbing fastest at the top of the distribution.

The Launch: Engineering Context for Leaders and Agents

LinearB has spent years collecting data from the tools engineers use every day, such as GitHub and Jira, while linking each code change to the ticket that requested it and the release that shipped it. Agentic Studio puts that history to work for managers, who can type a plain question such as where delivery is stuck or whether AI spending is paying off and receive an answer with a suggested next step.

Coding agents get the same history through an MCP server, which is a standard way for AI tools to plug into outside data, along with add-ons that LinearB calls agent skills. An agent about to edit a file can now see who owns that code, how often it has been rewritten and whether it caused recent incidents, which tells the agent how carefully it needs to work.

The first skill, called effort, is in early access and uses that history to decide how hard an agent should try on each change. A simple, low-risk edit gets a quick pass that uses fewer tokens, the units AI providers bill by, while a complex or risky change gets more effort with careful, tested edits. The skill works with any coding agent, Agentic Studio is available now to all LinearB customers and the next skills will focus on code review and merging.

Companies are pouring money into AI coding tools, with enterprises spending $4.0 billion on them in 2025 against $550 million a year earlier according to Menlo Ventures. That sevenfold jump makes coding the largest single use of AI inside companies, at 55% of the $7.3 billion spent on departmental AI.

MarketsandMarkets expects the market for AI code assistants to grow from $8.14 billion in 2025 to $127.05 billion by 2032, a rise of about 48% a year. As writing code gets cheaper, the pressure moves to everything that happens after the code is written, which is why the tools that measure engineering work are growing fast too, with Gartner estimating that category at about $400 million and expanding more than 40% a year.

The Delivery Bottleneck: Why We Have Larger Pull Requests and Longer Waits

More code does not mean faster delivery, because every change still has to be checked by a human reviewer before it ships. LinearB's 2026 Software Engineering Benchmarks Report, which covers 8.1 million pull requests from 4,800 teams in 42 countries, shows that AI-assisted changes run to 408 lines of code against 157 for changes written without AI, measured at the 75th percentile, which makes them 2.6 times larger (our arithmetic).

Changes written by agents face a different problem, since they wait 17.6 hours for a reviewer to pick them up against 3.4 hours for human changes, which is 5.2 times longer (our arithmetic). Once a reviewer starts, the review itself takes 6.4 hours, so an agent's change spends almost three times as long waiting in the queue as it does being read. Across the whole dataset 84.4% of changes written without AI were accepted within 30 days against 32.7% of AI changes.

Pull request size and review wait by type.

Output: Heavy AI Users Pull Ahead

The productivity gains are real for heavy users, since among the 83,000 developers in LinearB's 2026 AI benchmarks those who used AI on at least three out of every four coding days merged a median 95.7% more pull requests per week in May 2026 than in June 2025. Developers who used no AI at all merged 3.6% fewer over the same period.

The gains grow step by step with usage, with developers using AI on half their coding days gaining 65.4% and occasional users gaining 24.4%. LinearB says these figures show a correlation that does not prove AI alone caused the gains. It also notes that the acceptance rate of heavy users' changes slipped 4.4% over the year. AI use is now close to universal, with 88.3% of organizations using AI tools daily or weekly, yet 44.7% still do not measure what those tools deliver.

Merged pull request growth by AI usage band.

Adoption Depth: What Elite Organizations Do Differently

Even the best teams use AI less than the hype suggests. At elite organizations, the top 10% in LinearB's sample, AI helps write only 54% of pull requests, AI writes 45% of the code that gets merged and fully autonomous agents open just 4.7% of all changes.

The biggest difference between the best teams and the rest is AI code review, where an AI tool checks a change before a human does. Elite organizations use it on 57% of pull requests against 8% at fair organizations, the top 60%, which is a sevenfold gap. It is also the easiest win on the table, because changes with an AI review are accepted at the highest rate of any type, lifting acceptance by up to five percentage points, while LinearB's August analysis found a lift of two to three points across almost every type of change.

Output Against Token Cost

More AI output comes with a much bigger bill, since organizations merge 2.6 pull requests per developer each week, twice the 1.3 at fair organizations, yet spend $481 per developer each month on AI tokens against $50, which is 9.6 times as much.

In plain terms, doubling output has cost close to ten times as much in AI usage, which is the trade-off that boards and finance teams now ask engineering leaders to explain. LinearB labels these token figures as rough averages, though the direction is clear: this is the gap the effort skill is designed to narrow by saving expensive AI effort for the changes that need it.

Agent Yield and the Ownership Gap

Acceptance is where agents still fall short, since at elite organizations 79% of the changes opened by autonomous agents are merged within 30 days against 92% of changes written only by people, a gap of 13 points (our arithmetic).

The gap widens at weaker organizations, where agent acceptance drops to 58% at good organizations and 37% at fair ones, leaving agent work 28 and 44 points behind the overall rate (our arithmetic). LinearB's explanation is ownership, because a change that no developer feels responsible for often never gets merged. That is why Agentic Studio gives agents code ownership history, so an agent knows whose code it is touching before it opens a change.

Cost Control: Token Spend and the Effort Skill

Token bills are rising fastest among the heaviest users, since at the 90th percentile, meaning the top tenth of spenders, developers now use $35.20 of AI tokens per coding day, up nearly 75% in three months, while the typical developer's spend has barely moved. That works out to $481 a month or $5,772 a year per developer (our arithmetic), which LinearB says is still under 4% of what a developer costs in total.

Gartner expects spending on AI coding tools to pass the average developer's salary by 2028 as token use keeps climbing. LinearB's own worked example, which is an illustration and not customer data, shows why the cost of each delivered change matters more than the raw bill, since a 350-developer company that quadruples its token spend from $300,000 to $1.2 million a month while lifting output from 3.3 to 5.67 merged changes per developer each week cuts its cost per delivered change by 29%, from $864 to $613.

Customer Evidence: Kraken and Emburse

Kraken offers an early example of the data at work, since the company used LinearB's MCP server with an AI assistant to find out what was slowing its code reviews and learned that the cause was time zones and reviewer availability, not large changes. Over the next four months it cut its slowest review times, measured at the 90th percentile, by more than half.

Emburse uses the data at board level, with chief technology officer Ken Ringdahl putting LinearB charts directly into board decks because his board wants to know how the company uses AI and what return it gets. LinearB says its AI assistant and MCP access have the highest user retention of any features it has released.

LinearB plans its next agent skills for code review and merging, followed by tools that help teams govern AI-written code safely and cut what they spend on AI. Chief executive and co-founder Ori Keren describes the company's data as a knowledge graph of the entire software delivery process that coding tool makers do not have, while co-founder and chief operating officer Dan Lines says the goal is to move leaders from reading dashboards to knowing what to do next.

For engineering leaders, LinearB's data points to three places where AI coding is losing value today, which are the review queue, the agent change that nobody owns and the top of the token bill. Agentic Studio is LinearB's attempt to fix all three by giving people and agents the same context, in a market that Gartner sizes at about $400 million and growing more than 40% a year.

items.title: The New York Times Sues Brave Web Browser For AI Scraping, Bypassing Paywalls
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The New York Times and several other publishers have sued (PDF) Brave Software, accusing the browser maker of scraping their websites without permission and helping users bypass paywalls. The Verge reports: According to a complaint (PDF) filed by the companies that run New York Daily News, the Chicago Tribune, and the Orlando Sentinel, Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to "real-time online content from the Brave Index." The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to "respond to specific user queries," or both. Brave has allegedly provided "stolen copyrighted content" to "many" AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Brave also promotes "hundreds of top publishers" as being accessible through its "Paywall blocker" feature in its browser.
 
"Brave has never asked for the Publishers' permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies," the complaint says. "On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers' paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave's access to the Publishers' websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers' copyrighted content." "While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct," Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement. "We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world."

items.title: Microsoft's Canada Timezone Troubles Leave Admins Fixing Calendars, Pretending They're In Bogota
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Microsoft is scrambling to fix time-zone problems across Outlook, Power Automate, Fabric, SharePoint and other products after parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1. "The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up," reports The Register. From the report: Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack. Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change.
 
Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first. Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed.
 
Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already. SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12.
