items.title: How to Build Durable Chat Memory for RAG Using ScyllaDB and LangChain
items.author: ScyllaDB
items.content:
How to replace LangChain’s in-memory chat history with ScyllaDB — so your RAG chatbot retains context across restarts and scales across replicas

This post demonstrates how to integrate ScyllaDB Vector Search into your LangChain project for RAG use cases, as well as how to use ScyllaDB as a durable conversation memory within LangChain.

Large language models are trained on a fixed snapshot of the world. RAG patches that gap by retrieving relevant documents at query time and injecting them into the prompt. The pipeline has two phases:

  • load documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk, store embeddings in a vector store.
  • enrich and embed the user’s question, find the nearest vectors (ANN search), pass the matching chunks as context to the LLM.

But RAG alone is not enough. You still need to keep track of all inputs provided by the user.

LLMs are stateless. Every call starts with a blank slate unless you replay the conversation history. LangChain’s abstraction lets you plug in any backend as the storage layer for that history. The default in-memory implementation vanishes on process exit. A database-backed implementation survives restarts, scales across replicas, and lets you inspect or audit conversations later.

That’s where ScyllaDB comes in.

ScyllaDB is a NoSQL database optimized for high-throughput, low-latency workloads. Combined with LangChain, you can build reliable and always-on AI applications:

  • data is automatically replicated across nodes, so there is no single point of failure. The cluster continues serving reads and writes even if a node goes down.
  • ANN queries return results fast enough that retrieval doesn’t dominate your chain’s total latency.
  • add nodes to the cluster to increase throughput without schema changes or downtime.
  • a native type and HNSW index are created automatically in ScyllaDB.

In this example, embeddings are generated locally with sentence-transformers (, 384 dimensions). For production use, you can swap in OpenAI embeddings, Cohere, or any other provider supported by LangChain.

In each conversation turn, the chatbot is reading data from ScyllaDB and then writing back into it using LangChain.

With the release of ScyllaDB 2026.2, you can now integrate LangChain with ScyllaDB seamlessly by reusing the existing Cassandra connector.

pip install langchain langchain-community \
    sentence-transformers langchain-groq \
    langchain-text-splitters cassio \
    scylla-driver python-dotenv

Copy to and fill in your credentials:

# ScyllaDB Cloud
SCYLLADB_CONTACT_POINTS=node-0.your-cluster.cloud.scylladb.com
SCYLLADB_DATACENTER=AWS_US_EAST_1
SCYLLADB_USERNAME=scylla
SCYLLADB_PASSWORD=your-password-here
SCYLLADB_KEYSPACE=demo

# Groq (LLM)
GROQ_API_KEY=gsk_...

Retrieve the contact points, datacenter name, username, and password from the tab of your cluster in ScyllaDB Cloud.

Connect to ScyllaDB Cloud

from cassandra.cluster import Cluster
from cassandra.auth import PlainTextAuthProvider
from cassandra.policies import DCAwareRoundRobinPolicy
import cassio

cluster = Cluster(
    contact_points=["node-0.your-cluster.cloud.scylladb.com"],
    auth_provider=PlainTextAuthProvider(
        "scylla", "your-password"
    ),
    load_balancing_policy=DCAwareRoundRobinPolicy(
        local_dc="AWS_US_EAST_1"
    ),
)

session = cluster.connect()
cassio.init(session=session, keyspace="demo")

The call registers the session and keyspace globally so all downstream integrations (the vector store and the chat history) pick it up without further configuration.

Although cassio was originally built as a Cassandra integration, it is session-agnostic. It works with whatever driver session you hand it, so passing a session created by scylla-driver works just as well.

Integrating ScyllaDB with LangChain Vector Store

As an example, consider a chatbot that ingests articles, answers questions using retrieved context, and preserves conversation history in the database.

from langchain_community.document_loaders import WebBaseLoader
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
from langchain_community.embeddings import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
from langchain_community.vectorstores import Cassandra

loader = WebBaseLoader([
    "https://docs.scylladb.com/stable/get-started/scylladb-basics.html",
    "https://docs.scylladb.com/stable/get-started/data-modeling/query-design.html",
])
docs = loader.load()

chunks = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=500,
    chunk_overlap=50,
).split_documents(docs)

embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

vectorstore = Cassandra(
    embedding=embeddings,
    table_name="rag_docs"
)
vectorstore.add_documents(chunks)

retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(
    search_kwargs={"k": 4}
)

fetches and parses each URL into a Document.

RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter then breaks each document into 500-token chunks with a 50-token overlap so sentences are not severed at boundaries.

Cassandra(table_name="rag_docs") creates the table on first use, including a column (matching all-MiniLM-L6-v2’s output dimensions) and an HNSW index. Subsequent runs reuse the existing table; you only pay the embedding cost once unless you call again.

Persistent Chat Memory Implementation

from langchain_community.chat_message_histories import CassandraChatMessageHistory

def get_chat_history(session_id: str) -> CassandraChatMessageHistory:
return CassandraChatMessageHistory(
    		session_id=session_id,
    		table_name="chat_history",
	)

CassandraChatMessageHistory stores each message as a row keyed on . Because rows are written to ScyllaDB, the history survives process crashes, server restarts, and horizontal scaling. Any replica that opens the same sees the same history.

Change to start a fresh conversation. Keep it the same to resume where you left off — that is the entire persistence mechanism.

from langchain_groq import ChatGroq
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate, MessagesPlaceholder
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough
from langchain_core.runnables.history import RunnableWithMessageHistory

llm = ChatGroq(model="llama-3.3-70b-versatile")

ablePassthrough
from langchain_core.runnables.history import RunnableWithMessageHistory

llm = ChatGroq(model="llama-3.3-70b-versatile")

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
	("system",
 	"You are a helpful assistant. Answer the user's question using the "
 	"retrieved context below.\n\nContext:\n{context}"),
	MessagesPlaceholder(variable_name="chat_history"),
	("human", "{question}"),
])

chain = (
	RunnablePassthrough.assign(context=lambda x: "\n\n".join(
    	d.page_content for d in retriever.invoke(x["question"])
	))
	| prompt
	| llm
	| StrOutputParser()
)

chain_with_history = RunnableWithMessageHistory(
	chain,
	get_chat_history,
	input_messages_key="question",
	history_messages_key="chat_history",
)

config = {"configurable": {"session_id": "user-abc-session-1"}}

answer1 = chain_with_history.invoke(
	{"question": "What is the difference between a partition key and a clustering key in ScyllaDB?"},
	config=config,
)
print(answer1)

answer2 = chain_with_history.invoke(
	{"question": "How does using both keys affect the sort order of the data within a partition?"},
	config=config,
)
print(answer2)  # References the prior turn via memory

RunnableWithMessageHistorywraps the chain and automatically loads prior turns from before each call, then appends the new turn after. Both storage operations hit ScyllaDB.

The second question drills deeper into clustering columns introduced in the first answer. Without persistent memory, the LLM would have no context for what was already explained; with it, the conversation flows naturally across turns.

, the vector store:

CREATE TABLE demo.rag_docs (
	row_id      	text PRIMARY KEY,
	attributes_blob text,
	body_blob   	text,
	metadata_s  	map<text, text>,
	vector      	vector<float, 384>,
);

CREATE CUSTOM INDEX idx_vector_rag_docs ON demo.rag_docs (vector)
	USING 'vector_index';

CREATE INDEX eidx_metadata_s_rag_docs ON demo.rag_docs (ENTRIES(metadata_s));

, the message store:

CREATE TABLE demo.chat_history (
    partition_id  text,
    message_id    timeuuid,
    body_blob     text,
    PRIMARY KEY (partition_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

The full demo code is available on GitHub. You can run it once to ingest and embed the articles, then run it again with the same to verify that prior conversation turns are loaded from the database.

items.title: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered Is A Faithful, If Flawed, Remaster
items.author: Kurt Indovina
items.content:
Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a 3D brawler where you can play as Godzilla 1990, hurl Godzilla 2000 across a city, and then watch Anguirus drop kick him through a building. It's hilarious. That alone is a compelling sales pitch to have me and many other Godzilla fans say, "Why, yes, please take my money." It's a pitch that follows through on its promise, which shouldn't come as a surprise considering it plays one-to-one like the original 2002 game.

It's fun to wail on giant monsters as the city crumbles around them, and that fun factor only increases when playing locally with three friends--especially if you're playing on Nintendo Switch 2 where you can pop off a Joy-Con, hand it to the person next to you, and laugh maniacally when you throw them into a pool of lava on Monster Island.

It's just unfortunate that the game's simple, straightforward, arcade-like fun is hindered by hours and hours of grinding needed to unlock all the game's monsters, stages, and modes. Nor does the grind complement the game's pick-up-and-play design, turning a fun game that offers plenty of laughs into a laborious chore when all you want to do is play as Rodan. 

From the start, you have access to four of its 12 monsters: Godzilla 1990, Gigan, Megalon, and Anguirus. The four starting monsters showcase the variety in monster types, with the exception of flying ones like King Ghidorah and Rodan. Monsters generally have the same movesets, with some having a few extra tricks, like Gigan's ability to teleport or Megalon burrowing underground and grabbing its foe when it emerges. At first, monster movesets can feel samey, each one having identical combos, and similar effects like stomping on a foe's foot, or pressing back and kick at the same time to perform a drop kick. But there are small quirks and flourishes to each monster that make them unique from each other, like Anguirus's block, which sees them turn around, exposing their spiked back to an opponent's attack before stunning the enemy momentarily as they shake their mitts in a display of slapstick buffoonery.

While it isn't a deep fighting game, there's enough versatility and depth to sustain fun fights, like the ability to throw buildings or collect power-ups that call in Mothra for an air strike. The variety also ensures no two fights feel the exact same. Having four monsters running around the stage, blasting beams out of their mouths, tossing buildings, or rolling around endlessly to avoid each other is just fun. The experience can feel thin on your own, but with friends it's a romp, and that's owed to it being a very approachable fighting game. And even during the hours I've spent playing alone, the game still manages to get an occasional laugh out of me due to its cartoony kaiju violence.

It's just too bad that unlocking other monsters isn't as straightforward as in the original game. In the 2002 game, unlocking monsters simply required completing the game's Adventure mode, which was short and arcade-like, and saw you defeating one monster after another until facing off against Mechagodzilla in the end, rewarding you with a new playable character. In its place in the remaster are three forms of progression: character XP for each individual monster; Research Points, which complete Projects that in turn unlock characters and stages; and Rumors, objectives to fulfill in order to unlock Projects. All of these layers coalesce into an attempt to prolong the game's playtime and unlock your favorite monsters (like Rodan!), and it's for the worse.

In the 11 hours I've spent playing, the majority of that time has been alone trying to unlock characters, which I've yet to complete doing, with the remaining three being Destroyah, Mechagodzilla, and, yes, Rodan. Unlocking each monster requires a checklist of variables like winning 12 fights with either Megalon or Gigan, which in turn unlocks a Research Project, which progresses by playing Adventure modes or multiplayer battles (both online and locally). Completing Rumors and fulfilling Research quotas vary in time, and sometimes fulfilling them reveals Rumors and Research quotas needed to unlock a monster. I was misled a couple times thinking I'd only have to complete one Research to unlock Mecha-King Ghidorah, only to realize another Project would unlock first. This grind extends to the game's Adventure modes, which are locked behind an individual monster's level. It's exhausting.

The two new Adventure modes offer a welcome change up to the tried-and-true classic Adventure, with the addition of Adventure Gauntlet and Adventure Challenge. Gauntlet pits you against two CPUs that get more difficult with each round, and Challenge is an even harder version, where CPUs start with power-ups. It's too bad that unlocking these requires leveling up one monster at a time, and can be very time-consuming.

There is, however, a way to play all the monsters and stages without grinding: Tournament Mode. This mode is peculiarly tucked away in the settings rather than available in the main menu. Toggling this disables all modes except Custom Battle, and halts Research and Level progression. Here you can play as any monster in either a 1v1 match against a CPU, or with three other friends locally. Tournament Mode cannot be played online, meaning you're still stuck unlocking characters the boring way the game intended. Still, this mode is a saving grace that allowed me to finally play as Rodan and knock around Destroyah with my pals. It's a weird workaround, and one that wasn't made clear to me until after reaching out to the developers to see if the game had cheat codes of its own (the original game's codes do not work).

The game's grind feels more in line with what'd be expected in a modern live-service game, and while I'm thankful there are no microtransactions in this game, the game's inclusion of these systems puts it at odds with a game that celebrates pure and stupid fun.

Destroy All Monsters is a blast, and whether you're playing it in-person with friends or online, there are a lot of laughs to be had in the spectacle of watching giant kaiju fly through the sky. So despite the grind of its single-player modes, the joy of playing hadn't worn thin. 

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I'm glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats--not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding.

Just let me smash my toys together, please.

items.title: Itch Is Being Flooded By AI-Generated Garbage
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The number of game pages being created per-day on Itch has doubled, the indie games site announced Saturday on Bluesky. When asked why, they responded: "take a guess." 

As the gaming news site Aftermath puts it, "the surge has been almost entirely down to AI-created garbage racing onto the platform as the popularity of vibe-coded theft, copycats and machine-built slop explodes."



Back in 2024, when the spectre of AI-'created' video games was still in its infancy, indie platform itch.io decided that the best it could do to combat this growing threat was, like Valve has done with Steam, institute a voluntary 'AI' filter when adding new projects to the site. By November 2026, as itch buckles under the weight of new AI-generated 'games' pouring onto the site, that filter is proving about as robust as a wet paper bag.... Shopfronts are being deluged by this shit, and it's making it a terrible user experience for customers. 

 And while in Valve's case there's a compelling case for stronger human moderation of the store, I'm not sure that's a viable option for a relatively tiny, community-run platform like itch... [A]t time of writing I visited the latest releases section and there was still a huge number of clearly AI-generated titles (or titles making extensive use of AI in their visual assets) which made no use of itch's voluntary tag system. 

The issue here isn't that these games are making money--itch themselves say in a reply that while the number of projects listed has doubled, "the number of downloads and purchases has not"--it's that an inability to combat this surge makes the site worse for every single person using it. It gets harder to find real games, for example, and it also makes the shopfront look like a clearance rack.

items.title: Bad Flock Info Leads Police To Tow Wrong Car, Then Towing Company Totals It
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
"Police continue to blindly trust Flock cameras above and beyond the evidence in front of their own eyes," reports Jalopnik.com. 

"After incorrectly connecting Rosalyn Crump's car to a shooting that had occurred the previous day, police had her car towed and impounded as evidence, reports Moneywise..."

According to WWBT 12 On Your Side, Richmond, Virginia, police didn't have a license plate number for the suspect's car, making it impossible to search Flock's records for that plate. Flock cameras collect more than just license plate information, so police searched for a make, model, color, and approximate model year. Based on this extremely vague description, police zeroed in on Crump's 2012 Hyundai Elantra. Around 2 a.m. they started looking through the windows with flashlights to see what was in plain sight, which isn't technically a "search" — at least, not one that would require a warrant... [Crump was asleep, but left her home to speak to the police officers to tell them they had the wrong car. But they didn't believe her.] 

Other body cam footage shows an officer expressing doubt that Crump's car is the right one, since child seats and other items inside seem inconsistent with a shooting. Another officer replies, "Don't be surprised if they would have set that up like that." Instead of believing the evidence, or Crump, or interviewing witnesses who could have corroborated her story, police called Seibert's Towing to impound the car... 

[Later] Police identified a similar-looking car that seemed to be actually connected to the shooting, and released Crump's Elantra. Nobody actually told Crump this until four days later. Seibert's told Moneywise that police didn't actually release the car until then. Either way, they didn't tell her that Seibert's had ripped the front bumper off during the towing process — leaving the car undrivable — until she arrived to pick it up. Seibert's took responsibility for causing the cosmetic damage, and was willing to cover the $2,212.30 bill to paint and replace the bumper cover, fog lights, and wheel liners. Then Crump asked for a full mechanical inspection, which revealed damaged tie rods and ball joints, jacking the bill beyond $6,000. Seibert's says it didn't cause this damage. Regardless of how it occurred, Seibert's insurer and Crump agree that her Hyundai is now a total loss due to the cost of the repairs it needs. It had been drivable, if mechanically worn, before police ordered it towed, damaging it for nothing more than a case of mistaken identity. 
The president of Seibert's towing told Moneywise that while they'd originally offered $2,200 to repair the bumper damage, Crump must now negotiate with their insurance company. Crump has now resorted to a GoFundMe campaign to attempt to raise $17,100 for rental car expenses, a new car, and the expenses of moving to a different neighborhood. 130 donors have already contributed $7,431. 


Reached for comment, the Richmond Police Department told local newscasters they "understand that Ms. Crump did not ask to become part of this investigation," and that they recognize the "frustration of having a vehicle towed and subsequently damaged." But they also said they were following a "credible" lead, which is their responsibility. The department "appreciates Ms. Crump's cooperation" (and "sincerely hopes the remaining concerns about her vehicle can be resolved.") 

The city of Richmond has "already started backing away from Flock before Crump's story aired," reports Moneywise. "Mayor Danny Avula has decided not to renew Richmond's license plate reader deal with Flock, which ends June 30, 2027. As of September, the city had 99 Flock readers on its streets." 

They note that the Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm in Arlington, Virginia, "has tallied at least 27 cases since 2018" of similar police errors. "In each case, a license plate reader mistake led police to stop, jail or point guns at drivers who'd done nothing wrong. More than half came in 2023 or later."

items.title: Experts Expect 'Security Reckoning' As AI Tools Find And Exploit Software Bugs
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
The Washington Post reports:

Tens of thousands of South Koreans had their financial data exposed online in recent weeks after at least nine major banks there suffered cyberattacks that suggested a dark future for online security. One man, a 26-year-old living in southern China, was allegedly behind the attacks, according to an investigation by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike. Traces left online and failure to secure his own systems allowed investigators to piece together the man's name, age, location and what he allegedly did. The clues revealed that the devastating assault on some of Asia's most sophisticated financial institutions was the work of an amateur. The attacks were launched with help from a few artificial intelligence chatbots, CrowdStrike found, before asking one to help sell the stolen data online and draft a fake résumé touting cybersecurity skills... 

The hacker who broke into the South Korean banks had access to Anthropic's Claude, but because the U.S. firm's tools generally refuse to take illegal actions, free Chinese models were also used, including DeepSeek, CrowdStrike found. "The models are interchangeable," said Meyers, the CrowdStrike executive. 

The Post calls it "part of a wave of AI-enabled hacking that is advancing across the world, triggering alarm inside national governments as well as multinational companies."

"Basically any pedestrian, non-hacker can take these frameworks and start leveraging them to go after different targets," said Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike. The company has tracked an increase in the speed with which cyberattacks can move once inside a target's networks, as seasoned hackers and rank amateurs alike get a boost from AI tools. "Anyone can be a super-hacker now," Meyers said... Many cyber experts still expect the security reckoning to intensify as AI tools that can find and exploit software bugs become more widely distributed and understood. 

[Last] Monday, The Post reported that cybersecurity researchers from the start-up Cathedral who set out to test Anthropic's security found that they could access internal messages and meeting transcripts. Cathedral reported its findings to Anthropic, which said it resolved the newly discovered problems... Security experts say it's unlikely that any hacker is forgoing the use of AI tools right now. 
Even in America, critical infrastructure like energy and water companies need to be "immediately and comprehensively" tested for exploitable bugs, according to Snehal Antani, chief executive of cybersecurity company Horizon3. He tells the Post the government might need to fund that remediation, and even form "a public and private partnership to accelerate incident response."
